The study further investigated the impact of NRQCD corrections on the ${\cal B}(\eta_c)$ and ${\cal B}(\chi_{cJ})$ ratios.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casuals). Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly chose complex PINs to enhance security, casual users tended to select easy-to-remember ones for ease of use. To better protect casual users, who make up a substantial portion of the user base, it is essential to enhance the user experience by simplifying the setup process for these users.

This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently and precisely evaluate the integrals of products involving the solar irradiance function, as defined by ASTM standards, and user-defined smooth functions. The method's ability to produce accurate results with minimal evaluations is particularly beneficial due to the solar irradiance function's non-smooth, highly oscillatory nature. The accompanying Julia software facilitates the computation of solar-weighted quadrature rules across varying bandwidths or point counts. The described technique is anticipated to significantly aid solar-energy computations, where the user-defined function may involve complex and time-consuming calculations such as absorbance derived from solving Maxwell's equations.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation holds significant value in developing training algorithms for deep networks. However, current methods based on automatic differentiation and Kronecker-factored block diagonal approximations disregard noise in the data, leading to inaccuracies in capturing the network's intrinsic curvature. Our proposed ViViT method capitalizes on the low-rank structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton approximation, providing an accurate solution without the computational burdens associated with full-memory or KD-block diagonal approaches. Our technique enables efficient generation of the principal eigenvalue and eigenvector for the generalized Gauss-Newton Hessian, and can be utilized for defining curvature-based loss functions and adaptation in model optimization.

Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such gender-based distinctions are present in a language, related words must conform to the appropriate gender. For example, in Spanish, the noun "lampara" (a feminine object) when modified by "un," becomes "una lampara." In order to apply gender constraints to inanimate objects, a model must understand inanimate nouns and their grammatical gender. We investigate the effectiveness of pre-trained language models in achieving this understanding and the implications of gender bias in their representations. Our study centers on three core hypotheses: (a) representations of a noun and its feminine variant in a language with grammatical gender are equidistant from the feminine gender; (b) a sentence encoder trained on data from such a language accurately infers the grammatical gender of inanimate objects; and (c) an existing, highly advanced language model is itself susceptible to grammatical gender bias. We collected and annotated a dataset with over 5,000 unique base forms and more than 22,000 sentence examples derived from Wikipedia articles in six distinct languages. We employed this dataset to examine the representations and accuracy of two leading models, each fine-tuned on datasets that include the languages with grammatical gender. Our hypothesis tests were conducted through semantic similarity analyses using a range of metrics. We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain higher-level structure, we prove that the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, and have a certain complexity structure, exhibit rigidity as well.

Estimating an object's pose is a crucial part of most visual pipelines in robots and 3D vision as a whole. This study tackles the challenge of predicting a novel object's 6DOF pose without any prior training on it. This zero-shot or novel object pose estimation task is complicated by the large number of possible object categories. We address this challenge by using category-level information to expand the number of pose predictions we can accurately make. Unlike previous work, we do not require access to further 2D or depth image data for these novel objects. Instead, we rely solely on category-level information combined with 3D model data. This combination allows us to achieve a good prediction of the object's pose. Although we cannot directly compare our results to state-of-the-art methods due to their focus on many more precise metrics, our results show a good trade-off between precision and recall, and we outperform the baseline method used in this study. The code for this work can be accessed at: https://github.com/asharace/zero-shot-pose-estimation.

Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by using publicly available sparse data. Our team submitted a solution to the expanded challenge of predicting estimated time of arrival. Our method involves extracting multiple feature sets - node flow characteristics, segment-based attributes, and similarity-based properties, which we used to train a model based on decision trees with gradient boosting. Our results demonstrate exceptional predictive capabilities across three cities - London, Madrid, and Melbourne - and even surpass some graph neural network-based approaches in estimating travel times. Our source code is available at https://github.com/c-lyu/Traffic4Cast2022-TSE.

This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on past actions. Our experiments confirm that VACA effectively approximates various interventional and counterfactual scenarios in different real-world datasets.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant advancement in data rate complexity necessitates new recording techniques and systems. Our team successfully deployed a groundbreaking data recording system known as REALTA during an upgrade to the Cork station. This system is comprised of two high-performance recording systems, including the standard VNO and a more recent VNX type, alongside an innovative 32-channel, 16TB per day recording system. REALTA was utilized in two primary modes during initial testing: a 6.5 Tbit per day all-sky mode and a 1.5 Tbit per day focused 180-degree mode. We present the outcomes from these initial tests, encompassing 24 hours of continuous testing in both the all-sky and archive modes, a sample of around 32,000 individual images from the on-site system, and a discussion on future observing strategies for the facility.

In recent years, advancements in machine learning and deep learning technologies are significantly impacting photonic research. This involves exploring machine learning-driven approaches to develop and apply photonics across various key areas, such as designing metaphotonics, creating metaphotonics-based systems, developing artificial neural networks, and leveraging big data and optimization techniques. This article provides an overview of cutting-edge metaphotonics, focusing on cutting-edge advancements enabled by machine learning. It discusses specific applications and perspectives on integrating artificial intelligence into metaphotonics. Furthermore, it outlines future research directions and highlights challenging topics requiring immediate attention.

The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become a daunting task. In an effort to minimize financial losses, major film producers and studios continually seek a more reliable method for estimating movie revenue before making an investment. Researchers in this field face an additional hurdle: the scarcity of a large, contemporary dataset to work with. In an attempt to fill this void, our team has developed a more comprehensive, richer dataset collected from IMDb, which is designed to facilitate research and analysis. By aggregating summary data from over 7.5 million titles and detailed information for more than 200,000 films, our compiled dataset provides an indispensable resource for researchers and data analysts. Utilizing various statistical analysis methods, our findings reveal that a movie's star-studded cast or director contributes positively to revenue generation. We propose a new approach to evaluating the'star power' of a movie and have selected a set of relevant attributes as key features for revenue prediction. By employing machine learning algorithms to train on these attributes, we successfully categorize movies into 10 groups based on expected revenue, achieving a notable accuracy rate of 60%. Additionally, all generated datasets and analysis code are publicly accessible, as well as the source codes of our scraper bots, enabling other researchers to build upon and adapt our work.

The energy shift poses a threat to the stability of the power grid's operation, 
which necessitates maintaining both voltage amplitude and frequency within 
safe limits. Research has primarily concentrated on the stability and 
frequency dynamics but largely overlooked voltage stability. This work aims to 
investigate the stability of simple networks through both linear stability and 
bulk analysis, specifically evaluating how the secondary control for frequency 
guarantees the stability of a particular power grid and also noting an observed 
stabilizing influence on voltage dynamics despite only analyzing secondary 
frequency control.

Cyber Physical Systems are driving technological advancements and contributing to innovative solutions. A multi-faceted approach is essential to overcome the significant challenges in designing and developing these systems, especially from an engineering perspective. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modeling and integrating intelligent Cyber Physical Systems. The work is grounded in existing methodologies and utilizes a hierarchical Systems of Systems approach, incorporating an on-board agent to leverage full CPS potential. The proposed framework empowers adaptive decision making, facilitates conceptual modeling, and enables actionable engineering strategies. The effectiveness of this methodological framework was demonstrated through its practical application to a diverse set of scenarios.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized scattering signatures associated with a Compton process that might be producing UV and soft X-ray excess in certain blazars. Predictions are made about the polarization characteristics that polarimetry missions should detect for two specific blazars: AO 0235+164 and 3C 279.

In our study of intricate multi-dimensional potential patterns, specifically the
"swamp-parameter space" associated with the de Sitter conjecture, where we investigate
how the fundamental properties of these patterns change in a specific region, we utilize
a mathematical technique called analytic continuation to expand our understanding. 
This technique enables us to analyze continuously the changes in these patterns 
as we vary certain parameters in the "landscape," gaining insights that were previously unknown.

To develop optimal methods for identifying identical pure states with perfect accuracy using limited resources, we investigate optimal methods for recognizing identical states in a specific context.  By simplifying a complex problem through initial investigations into identical states that differ only in their relative phases, we gain valuable insights into the most effective strategies for the broader case where state identities are ensured through the inclusion of incoherent mixtures.  Notably, our research reveals that the most efficient approach for identifying any pair of pure states involves performing continuous measurements on a single system at specific intervals.  Furthermore, the associated measurement times that maximize the success probability of identifying two pure states correlate with the peaks of specific mathematical functions, namely the Airy function for pairs of states with identical coefficients and a hybrid of the Airy and Jagert functions for pairs of states with unequal coefficients.

Baryon production is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryon creation is attributed to the breaking of chiral symmetry through a process controlled by a temperature-dependent function. Utilizing lattice QCD results, the functions related to quark and gluon fragmentation are derived. It's found that three quark fragmentation dominates at low temperatures, whereas gluon fragmentation prevails at high temperatures. This model's findings on baryon production are then compared to data from ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions.

In the study of the sun's interior using sound waves, the speed of these waves when moving along the same meridian in opposite directions helps scientists understand the movement of the sun's fluid surface horizontally from the north to the south.  Researchers observed that the longitudinal averages of the speed of these waves change in response to the solar cycle, appearing as a 6.5-year oscillation in the period of time. The specific areas in the sun's active regions where the waves move faster than usual, the surrounding areas of these regions where the waves move slower than usual, and the large-scale flows beyond these regions all contribute to this oscillation. The new findings indicate that the majority of the oscillation comes from the large-scale flows outside active regions, whereas the oscillation caused by the active regions themselves is slower and several days old. The speed of these waves also affects the analysis of the sun's fluid surface using the helioseismic direct approach for estimating the meridional flow in the sun's interior. The current observations support theories that the sun's fluid surface moves with a periodic rate of about one rotation per 146 days. The new findings indicate that the solar cycle affects the solarity in different ways than previously thought and these effects change with the solar cycle.

Researchers from the NANOGrav, Parkes, European, and International Pulsar Timing Array Collaborations have discovered strong evidence suggesting a single source for background noise observed across multiple frequency ranges, which might be linked to the presence of stochastic gravitational waves within the frequency range of 1--100 nHz. They have considered a hypothetical scenario in which these waves originate from early turbulence in the universe brought on by non-helical magnetic fields at the energy scale of the quark confinement phase transition.  To investigate this phenomenon further, researchers used magnetic hydrodynamic simulations to observe the dynamic evolution of the magnetic field and compute the resulting gravitational wave output. They discovered that the simulated gravitational wave spectrum can be accurately modeled when the magnetic anisotropic stress is assumed to be consistent over time frames corresponding to the magnetic eddy turnover times. They developed a corresponding analytical spectrum featuring a frequency-related break that aligns with numerical simulations results.  To further study this phenomenon, researchers have analyzed the observed signal from Pulsar Timing Arrays, which helped to restrict parameters including generation temperatures ranging from 1--200 MeV, a magnetic field amplitude above 1% of the energy at the generation time, and a magnetic characteristic scale above 10% of the horizon scale.  Furthermore, researchers have discovered that the magnetic turbulence in question could lead to magnetic fields at the recombination epoch that alleviate Hubble tension. They suggested that these effects can be investigated further through joint experiments like the Cosmic Microwave Background measurements and gravitational

Light field technology has the potential to restore the visual characteristics of natural vision by capturing and reproducing the complete spatial and angular properties of light. However, the massive amount of data it generates in imaging processes makes it prone to compression issues, particularly in applications like microscopy, where significant improvements have been observed but are hindered by the current state of compression methods. Most existing approaches either use texture features or 4D compression techniques, but these have significant limitations including high complexity and insufficient attention to pixel disparity. To address this, a new, trainable framework is proposed, incorporating a disparity model that incorporates the propositions of the Willett et al. paper and an enhanced latent representation, as it combines local image details with coarse overall patterns. The framework also utilizes an optimized encoder, an enhanced latent representation, and a refined decoder to overcome previous limitations. By combining these elements, a novel, modular light field image compression approach is developed, along with an extensive set of experiments and benchmark tests using various benchmark datasets, showing improved performance across several metrics, including PSNR, MS-SSIM, and FID, at equal bitrates, with particular enhancements in microscopy images.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. Weighed against retrieval accuracy and 
computational efficiency, each type has its strengths and weaknesses. This study 
investigates combining the benefits of these two approaches by creating a hybrid 
model that utilizes the initial non-interactive embedding to generate a search 
space and then employs an interactive model, such as denoising autoencoders, 
within that space to refine the representation. We call this strategy NA2IE, 
and similarly, other composite models like IA1NE and IA2IE are devised. Our 
experiments conducted on a 100-language dataset demonstrate the superiority of 
the proposed hybrid models, particularly IA2NE, which combines the high accuracy 
of interactive and non-interactive models with the substantial decrease in 
computational requirements of non-interactive models.

The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic studies at the global, national, and local levels. Small-area estimates, generated through synthetic approaches, are crucial in addressing data shortages; however, the feasibility and effectiveness of different designs and modeling strategies are poorly understood in low-and-middle-income countries. In our research, we evaluate the strengths and limitations of various study designs, including cluster, migration, and two-stage approaches, in a real-world setting within Nigeria. Through simulations based on actual data, we evaluated synthetic estimators in isolation and in conjunction with hot-deck and ratio estimation techniques. Our findings suggest that cluster designs are generally the most reliable methods, although optimal results are achieved through the combination of efficient estimation modeling. We observed that the cluster design was the most reliable method, although a migration design performed relatively well for very local observations. The objective of this study is to propose a semi-classical model representing betting situations where the gambler's winnings are encoded in a quantum memory's intrinsic properties, rather than the conventional payout. We associate the initial investment with a single quantum system's ergotropy - a measure equivalent to the quantum analogue of free energy, as described by Allahverdyan, Balian, and Nieuwenhuizen - and express it through electromagnetic radiation. As betting outcomes occur, this system experiences attenuation and amplification, simulating loss and winning conditions. This stochastic evolution in the quantum memory is analogous to the random lasing phenomenon and can be characterized in a Bosonic Gaussian channel framework. We also extend the principles of the Kelly Criterion by identifying the optimal betting strategy for a given fixed odds and winning probability, then calculate the asymptotic doubling rate. Furthermore, by assuming that the input capital is a Gaussian density matrix - that is, a displaced, squeezed thermal Gibbs state - we investigate how model performance changes based on this state and conclude that the gambler should initially dedicate all resources to the coherent amplitude of the state.

Building on the recently created two-dimensional semiconductor MoSi$_2$N$_4$, our comprehensive study of band alignment in A$_2$Z$_4$ compounds explores quasiparticle band mapping in detail. By combining band alignment and stacking-dependent exciton analysis across different stacking orders, we establish fundamental guidelines for creating stable and consistent two-dimensional semiconductors of various types. Through theoretical calculations, we identify the inherent charge transfer between Z and A atoms as the primary driving force behind the strong in-plane and out-of-plane chemical bond strength in the tetragonal crystal structure of A$_2$Z$_4$ compounds. These interactions contribute to the unusually large bulk band gap of 3.18 eV in MoSi$_2$N$_4$, as well as the stacking-independent exciton of 2.05 eV, distinguishing it from other two-dimensional semiconductors like MoGe$_2$N$_4$ and MoGe$_2$As$_4$. These unique properties, coupled with the easy creation of monolayer MoSi$_2$N$_4$ films on substrates like SiO$_2$, make A$_2$Z$_4$ compounds exceptional candidates for highly efficient electronic devices and optoelectronic systems.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

The magnetic field and non-ideal factors are known to be pivotal in the process of stellar formation, but due to simplicity, hydrodynamics models often take precedence over more accurate representations like the alpha-disk model in disk studies. Efforts to bridge the gap between core collapse and mature disk development have been minimal. Our study reexamines the assembly of the protoplanetary disk through high-resolution 3D MHD simulations that incorporate ambipolar diffusion and comprehensive radiative transfer. We observe the disk's formation from the evolutionary trajectory of a prestellar core under realistic conditions. Our results contrast with the traditional magnetic field dominance in disk models due to the low efficiency of ambipolar diffusion during prestellar core collapse; as a result, the magnetic energy is lower than in earlier studies. The protoplanetary phase is marked by the disk's inner layer becoming increasingly influenced by radiation pressure and the host star's influence, suppressing magnetic energy generation. We find the alpha-disk model unsuitable for this phase, but see potential for a disk-stratified core and the presence of a massive, low-density envelope that warrants consideration in future simulations.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the visible to near-infrared spectrum (0.38 - 2.5 $\mu m$) using cross-dispersion spectrographs on two telescopes, one with 3.6 m and one with 7.8 m diameters. Our results indicate considerable variations in atmospheric models relative to measurements, particularly at lower altitude layers. This highlights issues with existing designs of ADCs for large telescopes. We've also proposed a new method for identifying the atmospheric parameters that control dispersion and demonstrated its accuracy.

This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and often overlook redundant input variables, which contribute nothing or negatively affect predictive power. By integrating the hierarchical latent variable model with multiple transition periods and a Bayesian neural network equipped with Horseshoe priors as the input layer, our proposed method effectively filters out irrelevant variables, enabling enhanced dependency capture across varying temporal resolutions. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world data reveal a substantial improvement in modeling and prediction accuracy for multi-period time series data with our proposed method.

In a setting that combines continuous logic, we establish a connection between Stone duality and Pontryagin duality by treating Pontryagin duality as a particular instance of Stone duality. This is achieved in the context of a topological abelian group $A$, and its associated group $\mathcal F$ of continuous homomorphisms from $A$ to the circle group $\mathbb T$, where $(A,+)$ along with $\mathcal F$ form a continuous logic structure $M. Consequently, the local type space $S_\mathcal F(M)$ directly corresponds to the Pontryagin dual of the group $\mathcal F$ if it is viewed as a discrete group. Furthermore, employing the correspondence established between compact and discrete abelian groups through Pontryagin duality, it follows that the local type space $S_\mathcal F(M)$ represents the Bohr compactification of the given topological group $A$.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To resolve these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a comprehensive ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

We propose a supersymmetric expansion of a basic $U(1)_X$ model with a new, $Z_2$ symmetry, where $U(1)_X$ is identical to $U(1)_{B-L}$. This model introduces a right-handed neutrino as a dark matter candidate. Since the model has only one expanionless $U(1)_X$ gauge field, it allows for a $U(1)_X$ breaking via a very small, naturally-generated gauge kinetic factor. However, this does not impact the dark matter stability or discoveries awaiting the HL-LHC and ILC at the TeV scale.

We investigate a smart reflecting surface-aided wireless-powered communication network where a multi-antenna energy transmitter broadcasts an exclusive energy signal to a powered transmitter, which then receives the energy and participates in a subsequent multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MUMM) communication task, obstructed by a strong, interfering signal from an external source. Due to the complex optimal solution nature, arising from non-convex optimization problems, caused by the reflection matrix dependence on energy reception of the powered transmitter, a novel, unsupervised deep learning approach is proposed. The proposed method effectively identifies the optimal weight matrices in a pre-trained network framework, yielding a close approximation to the optimal, limited by computational complexity constraints. Additionally, it is applicable to diverse energy receiver types and reduces energy waste resulting from sub-optimal initial positions. The efficiency of the proposed method is supported by numerical results showing its superiority over a baseline, conventional method.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. Prolate components dominated both parent and daughter nuclei for the experimental beta strength, while an upper limit was set for the oblate component in the parent state. To analyze the data, a minimum of three consecutive beta decay states was required for both progeny orientations, indicating prolate-dominated structures in both. The calculation that accounted for a broad range of QRPA configurations resulted in the calculation of the experimental beta strength, with the exception of the daughter's oblate component, which was not accounted for in the present study. The half-life measured in this study, 87.2 ms, along with the multi-component decay scheme, suggests the merit of incorporating $^{186}$Hg in experiments as a test bed for understanding beta decays in complex, real-time systems.

We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, a fermionic dark matter particle, and two additional scalar fields beyond the Standard Model. The interaction between these scalar fields influences both the dark matter relic density and the connection between right-handed neutrinos and dark matter. Our analysis centers around a resonant leptogenesis mechanism that produces baryon asymmetry through TeV-level right-handed neutrino masses. A viable parameter space is established to satisfy relic density, leptogenesis, and dark matter requirements simultaneously. Our findings reveal that dark matter relic density is a pivotal factor in this model, strongly interlinking with both the baryon asymmetry and the leptogenesis parameters. This underscores the significance of baryon asymmetry in driving dark matter relic density in this model. Additionally, we demonstrate that while dark matter direct detection may not be able to pinpoint the model's features, a multimuon detector could potentially verify the model's presence by searching for both dark matter and neutrino-related signs.

We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and the system's general properties. The algorithm essentially finds the best possible solution to an optimization problem by gradually improving an approximate solution based on the available information. The proof of its performance guarantees involves reinterpreting the original optimization problem in a way that can be efficiently solved using an iterative algorithm with a reduced complexity. The effectiveness of this algorithm has been demonstrated through successful simulations of controlling robots that can move in different environments under gravity's influence. The simulations show the algorithm's ability to adapt to unknown swimming, flying, and walking dynamics after seeing the system's behavior for just one trial.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit ward identities that extend those of Liouville theory. Specifically, for the Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ theory, new ward identities have been derived which are based on the su(3) current algebra, facilitating a comprehensive study of this model when coupled with a metric that has a conical singularity. Moreover, the ward identities of the Toda theory are consistent with the theory of free fermions, thereby providing a concrete framework for studying four-point correlation functions in this model. Consequently, the Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ theory has been shown to satisfy a metric-based scaling limit of the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ non-rational conformal field theory.

Despite significant advancements in producing realistic images with GANs, a major challenge persists in training the model, particularly with Inception training, which often results in the loss becoming stagnant in the high 0.5 to 0.6 range and failing to progress further. This issue is more prevalent in high-resolutionmissions. Our solution lies in incorporating the relation network into GANs, which enables better discriminative capabilities through the representation of feature distances. However, the original relation network technique introduces additional issues during training, such as mode collapse, a major concern in GANs. To address this problem, we have modified the original technique to employ triplet loss instead, which yields superior performance and training stability. Our experiments show that this improvement is not merely a side effect of utilizing larger batch sizes or higher training datasets. Additionally, we have introduced an innovative update rule, which allows triplet loss to be computed on a per-image basis, promoting the discovery of diverse training samples. Our findings indicate that incorporating the relation network through triplet loss is extremely effective in achieving consistent and significant improvements in both generative and discriminative capabilities, as demonstrated by a range of state-of-the-art results on high-resolution image synthesis tasks.

A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been introduced in the form of Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our approach categorizes time into two distinct frameworks: reference frames and quantum frames. Reference frames serve as a basis for establishing a universal phase reference, allowing us to achieve TF-QKD without the use of phase locking. Through data post-processing and an efficient fast Fourier transform-based algorithm, the phase reference can be reconciled efficiently. As a result, TF-QKD without phase locking is both cost-effective and efficient. Furthermore, our method enables a continuous variable system to operate at a significantly extended distance of 238 km. This innovation offers a widespread and practical solution for quantum communication applications across significant distances.

In this study, we identify the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz operators on the p-Fock space and the p-Bergman space, effective for p being greater than 1. To achieve this goal, we utilize novel relations between Riemannian surface mechanics and spectral analysis on complex line segments, drawing also on a crucial result previously achieved by an author. These findings have a natural extension in the context of classical function theory, leading to novel identifications regarding the algebras of bounded and continuous functions on the unit ball in higher dimensions.

Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. However, their effectiveness is restricted by the relatively small number of base categories used for training. To mitigate this constraint, we present a technique to automatically produce pseudo annotations of diverse objects using image-caption pairs and segmentation-prediction models. This technique then employs these pseudo labels for training object detectors, leading to notable improvements in object detection accuracy on various benchmarks. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary object detectors by significant margins, with performance boosts of up to 8% AP on the COCO novel category dataset and others. Code implementing this method is available for download on the GitHub repository 'PB-OVD'.

A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud produces a significant HII region and a photodissociation cavity, forming in an egg-like shape. This unique structure is studied using VLA radio observations from 1993 and ATCA spectral data from 1990, as well as BICE H2 mapping from 2001 and FORS H-alpha mapping from 2004. A combination of these observations reveals a 300,000 M sun protostellar disk and an expanding, 6 km/s shock wave in the surrounding material. This phenomenon is a result of the star's strong wind or a collision with another cloud. The disk's emission is the primary source of the radio continuum, contributing up to 50%. Until it collapses or undergoes a binary merger, this system will persist as a source of far-infrared emission for millions of years. This extensive system is largely enveloped by a 5 minute of arc (8000 au) neutral gas cloud, identified through its S-abundance and low ionization, containing "cold" (50K) material with solid dust grains three minutes of arc in diameter.

The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely on minimal inductive biases in their design, making them ideally suited for set-function applications. Moreover, their straightforward architecture allows for seamless processing of diverse modalities such as images, videos, and text. Due to their strengths, Transformer models have found successful applications in various computer vision tasks such as image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, and activity recognition. This review aims to provide an in-depth overview of Transformer models in computer vision, encompassing their various implementations and the emerging trends in this field.

Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of variables such as advancements in medical treatment and environmental shifts. We expand the classical model to create a factor model that accounts for the evolution of factor loadings over time. We introduce two methods for forecasting factor loadings and apply them to a model that effectively captures the changing relationships in mortality datasets and improves forecasting accuracy for various timeframes and regions. Moreover, a new technique based on analyzing critical points is developed to identify optimal forecasting intervals for long-term and short-term predictions, and simulated studies verify the performance of the model in multiple scenarios.

Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different child models is a popular strategy. However, due to interference issues, the performance of the searched models is often subpar when compared to traditional NAS methods. Current approaches tackle interference by increasing model complexity, narrowing the search space, or enhancing data diversity. However, these solutions either elevate training costs or compromise representation capability. In this paper, a comprehensive investigation is conducted into the underlying causes of interference and its associated problems. An novel architecture search framework, NAS-MMT, is then proposed to counter interference through memory mechanism design. Specifically, a problem-aware memory mechanism is introduced to minimize interference, while a reference memory mechanism is utilized to counter interference through matching low-probability high-accuracy targets. NasNet and ResNet are employed as test models to validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, while leveraging weighted ensemble and pruning tasks to further strengthen the results. Extensive experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework, yielding state-of-the-art performance without accommodation for hyperparameter adjustment.

Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed and measured. One common technique for evaluating the characteristics of these data sets involves computing multiple statistical measures or features, which can then be represented as a feature vector for analysis. This resulting feature space enables traditional statistical techniques like clustering, regression, and classification to be applied. Multiple open-source libraries are available to extract these features, including ones written for languages like Python and R, but they come with challenges such as a lack of single unified access point, need to switch languages, and limited supporting methodologies for analysis. This paper addresses these issues with an R-based tool called theft. This tool creates a unified framework for computing features across multiple popular feature extraction libraries and also develops a systematic approach for analyzing the resulting feature spaces. Its capabilities for automatic data alignment and mapping feature names to/extras enable smooth data translation between different analysis tools. Its core purpose is to facilitate data-driven decisions by providing a comprehensive view of the data.
We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary.

Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, negotiate translation contracts, and evaluates human translator proficiency.  Despite its importance, little research exists using quantitative methods to determine TQA's reliability.  In this study, we employ Bayesian Statistics to evaluate various TQA methods in both their original and adapted forms using original texts.  Utilizing six diverse TQA methods with both augmented and uncomplicated formats, we examine the effect of text type and evaluate several TQA techniques.  Our results indicate that several TQA measures are reliable for assessing human translators, with the assessment of multiple TQA methods and texts having high consistency.  Our findings also reveal that the reliability of TQA measures correlates with the agreement levels among human assessors.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering configuration related to energy distribution within a volume. It is found that specific ratios of eigenvalues are either zero or singular, and a range for these ratios within -1 and 1 is also established, and a formula for the total number of positive eigenvalues related to energy eigenchannels in certain cases is also derived. 

The constraints and formulas determined could impact areas such as imaging, sensing, and drug delivery as they provide correlative relationships between scattering matrices and various parameters such as volume energy distribution, and time, and this could lead to new applications for ideal and non-ideal confinement of waves.

We've found that using pruning methods on artificial neural networks significantly
reduces their size while maintaining their performance, and the optimal filter shape
depends on the data. For complex image data, a convolutional structure tends to
produce better results than a fully connected one. The reason for this is that
convolutional networks utilize a more efficient method of feature extraction that
takes into account data spatial relationships. The success of these networks is due
to more than just their reduced size - even when we remove their "training data", 
their performance remains substantial. The size of a neural network model alone is
not enough to guarantee its effectiveness in enhancing the limited performance of
other models, and their optimal structure will depend on the specific characteristics 
of their input data. The best performing subset of a neural network, known as the
"lottery ticket", is almost always a successful model, and its optimal composition 
largely predicts its ability to improve the limited performance of other models with
similar characteristics.

In lotteries with exceptionally large jackpots, as seen in Mega Millions and Powerball,
increasing bettor participation actually works to reduce the return on investment for each ticket.
The reason for this is a higher likelihood of multiple people winning with the same ticket.
In an effort to boost the return on a lottery ticket, we suggest an alternative approach.
By dividing the possible winning combinations among different vendors and pairing them,
we minimize the chance of multiple people sharing the same winning ticket.
The results show that our strategy successfully raises the return on a lottery ticket
without increasing the size of the grand prize.
Additionally, we've found the ideal time to maximize profits from ticket sales.
Interestingly, we've found that our strategy generates revenue in a manner opposite of the standard method,
where we maximize profits when the jackpot size is at its smallest in the standard method,
but the standard method generates more profits when the jackpot size is at its largest in our method.
Conversely, the standard method fails to generate profits when the jackpot size is at its largest in the standard method,
but the standard method succeeds in generating profits when the jackpot size is at its smallest in our method.

The large-charge expansion technique opens up a new possibility for calculating critical properties of high-charge operators $\phi^Q$, where the charge $Q$ is fixed. For operators of a given charge, the mathematical structure of their critical properties can be determined in the weak coupling regime by performing a series of calculations at fixed $Q$. When calculating at the six-loop level, new and complex diagrams that involve five or more legs need to be taken into account - these were previously unencountered in theoretical scalar-field calculations. Our research involves finding the critical properties of an operator with charge $Q=5$ at the six-loop level, complemented by existing information for operators of smaller charges. Alongside these calculations and the large-charge expansion, our study allows us to derive general expressions for the critical properties of all $Q$ values. Furthermore, our results enable the comparison of our findings in the strong and weak coupling regimes - this led to the derivation of critical values at which both results match, while also allowing us to determine the critical value above which the large-charge expansion and charge-dependent corrections apply. For the operator in question, our research involves calculating its six-loop critical charge, which accurately describes its critical behavior in the $O(N)$ symmetric model for an $N=4$ system. Our results confirm that our third-order renormalization-group analysis was accurate and provide new insights, allowing us to confidently apply the large-charge expansion to systems with even higher $N$.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that two mechanisms, cone tilt
and deformation potential, yield analogous effects on valley Hall responses.
However, this equivalence does not apply when the coupling involves position-dependent
velocity of electrons. The presence of a significant valley Hall effect near a
neutral charge condition in the isotropic scenario mirrors that seen with changes
in bond lengths, while in the anisotropic scenario, geometric transport characteristics
are anticipated similar to those induced by deformation potentials.
Investigating non-adiabatic dynamics, specifically within the regime of large
phonon frequencies, discloses a novel effect where inter-valley transitions are
stimulated through the mechanism of phonon-assisted scattering. The induced valley
Hall effect is predicted to significantly diminish with an exponential rate of
phonon frequencies. Conversely, this effect is anticipated to be significantly
muted in materials exhibiting a gapped phonon spectrum.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge seeks unsupervised domain adaptation for industrial waste sorting in semantic segmentation tasks, where we proposed the SIA_Adapt model. Combining several domain adaptation methods, SIA_Adapt's key strength lies in its ability to efficiently train on limited labeled data from new domains, due to its lightweight and adaptable structure. Key components of our approach include a novel adaptation loss, SwinVGG feature extraction, and a lightweight label propagation method. We successfully demonstrated the effective application of unsupervised domain adaptation techniques to the waste sorting task, achieving the top challenge performance. Our full model source code will be publicly available on the competition's platform after the challenge concludes.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing an iterative procedure, it achieves more effective embeddings than the conventional t-SNE method when working with such data types, as shown through its simulation on sample datasets.

We investigate the characteristics of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model, where a single impurity is attracted to a sea of Fermi particles, under conditions where their interactions have negligible spatial range. Our analysis utilizes the powerful tool of diagrammatic Monte Carlo, enabling us to explore an expansive diagrammatic series up to high orders, and evaluate the importance of simultaneous electron-hole pair corrections. In this study, the ground state energies of both the polaron and the molecule as a function of interaction strength are quantified, revealing an intricate interplay of the effects of pair correlations that deviate from both simple mean-field and poplar "intrinsically attractive" polaron theories. Our computational method is capable of accurately exploring diverse diagrammatic subspaces, even in extremely high orders, and we specifically examine the roles of spin and spatial symmetries in the system's behavior. Our final calculations investigate the polaron's quasiparticle mass and the molecule's binding energy, and how these properties vary with interaction strength. Our analysis also highlights a striking asymmetry in the behavior of the molecule's binding energy, and attributes it to the breakdown of the Bose approximation, and the corresponding changes in the diagrammatic series.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without optical elements, thanks to its versatility. By utilizing entangled analog quantum circuits, digital analysis and control can be combined, enabling a new method of quantum computing. Our research demonstrates that this method is particularly suitable for simulating fermionic systems. Since digital gates have a limited lifespan, these entangled analog circuits can be used to create a fermionic wave function without the need for optical circuits. Our study shows that this method is feasible with current experimental capabilities and we even propose a specific application using only 4 qubits. This research has the potential to lay a foundation for simulating fermionic systems in the future.

Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algebraic formulas describing various graph characteristics and encoding multiple graph invariants through their evaluation processes. Certain graphs, including complete and bipartite structures, can be identified through matching polynomial properties and relationships with established polynomial sets. The chromatic polynomial evaluated at -1 reveals the count of a specific graph orientation type. This study focuses on a general theorem involving families of graphs, which can be characterized through polynomials with established linear recurrence relations. This finding provides numerous applications in characterizing graph families with invariant-type properties. The work also offers an alternative to previously developed complex methods in graph theory, presenting a simpler approach to addressing similar problems.

We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending from the moduli space of genus two curves to a 10-fold cover of a Teichmueller curve, which was first found by Veech. Subsequently, we develop an expression in terms of iterated integrals that describes the monodromy representation of this connection. Consequently, as a secondary result, we determine the quantum representations of a vast array of pseudo-Anosov elements in the genus two mapping class group.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from top companies in the top 10 largest European IT-producing countries. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Our findings have practical implications for companies adopting Scrum projects during periods of voluntary, forced or anticipated remote working. They suggest that implementing successful hybrid working policies requires striking a balance between flexibility and oversight. Companies can build upon these parameters to develop effective home working and team collaboration policies, ultimately influencing project outcomes.

The concept of dichotomous matrices serves as an expanded interpretation of Hermitian matrices, with newly formulated guidelines identifying which arrowhead matrices fit this classification. Furthermore, specific conditions were derived to ensure unitary irreducibility of these matrices, and their maximum orthonormal vector count was calculated in relation to boundary numerical range, a criterion used in classification. This research enabled a comprehensive matrix classification based on the aforementioned Gau-Wu numbers.

In a study using the ALICE detector at the LHC, scientists investigated the elliptical movement of electrons created when beauty particles decay at a specific point near the centre of a collision between lead nuclei at a high energy level. These electrons were tracked in a data set involving nearly 22 million collisions. A comparison of their behaviour with that of prompt electrons produced directly in collisions showed a significant difference. These results are important as they may offer insights into how beauty particles behave in an environment with a non-uniform flow pattern. A calculation suggests that the observed effect is not due to a significant interaction between beauty particles and the elliptical flow pattern.

In pursuit of breakthroughs in the medical field, we analyze chromatic configurations in three-dimensional space, employing topological concepts. Building on Munkres' concept of alpha-complexes, we adapt its definition to accommodate color assignments while maintaining compatibility with existing properties. To effectively capture intricate point distributions, we introduce the concept of'support set,' utilizing the Delaunay tessellation for efficient computation. A color-based version of the chromatic alpha-plex is derived from its colored counterpart by filtering points based on their assigned colors. Utilizing the concept of 'color class' for each color assignment, we define the chromatic alpha-complex as a structural framework. A novel homology computation method is proposed for the complex, along with simulations that demonstrate its efficacy in distinguishing distributions of increasing complexity.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in interference networks containing $K$ transceivers. By investigating the extremal GDoF gain in various network configurations, we found that its value falls within the range of the mathematical expressions $\Theta(\sqrt[4]K)$ and $\Theta(2^{\sqrt{K}})$. We also offered a new binary power control strategy alongside bounds on the extremal gain, thus providing the limits of the range. Ultimately, the problem of determining the exact extremal GDoF gain for large values of $K$ remains open.

Auditing business processes often requires categorization of complex data.
Weighted bipartite graphs can efficiently represent transactions between
financial accounts, allowing us to apply methods from formal concept analysis.
The introduced methodology provides a transparent categorization of business
processes, using formal concept analysis and formal contexts. Unlike some
machine learning methods, this approach is explainable, making it suitable for
clustering on accountable principles. The focus is on developing categorization
schemes according to various agents' or sub-tasks' levels of interest in specific
financial transactions, using their professional roles as 'judges'. This study
combines two theories: Dempster-Shafer theory for defining categories and
formal concept analysis for creating the resulting categories. The proposed
methodology can handle any graph, including those with an incomplete set of
financial transactions, thanks to the framework's adaptability. The framework's
ability to classify nodes in different categories is justified using the principles
of informal reasoning and the framework's definitions. The framework's
implementations in Python, along with example usage, are available on
GitHub at the following location: 
https://github.com/UtrechtUniversitySCC/fca-dempster-shafer.

The Strauss process is a point process, and its density is unnormalized relative to a Poisson point process, incorporating a weighting factor lambda, between zero and one, which is applied to each pair of points closer than a certain distance, denoted as 'r'. Traditional techniques like basic acceptance-rejection algorithm fail to yield satisfactory results for this specific problem. However, we can generate random points on this specific process using techniques derived from a non-standard Poisson process called the "influence R-process", incorporating the concepts of "stitching". This method involves combining smaller "boring" point processes to create a single "stunning" point process, where the basic acceptance-rejection algorithm provides an efficient solution when applied to the larger process generated through "stitching".

In the context of string theory and quantum gravity, the Generalized Uncertainty Principle emerged as a key concept, leading to the deformation of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. The GUP has the potential to alter fundamental transformations, specifically Galilean and Lorentz transformations, resulting in the emergence of novel effects at the Planck scale. This study investigates the modification of GUP effects on Lorentz transformation along the x-axis and identifies similar effects in relativistic length measurements, highlighting their disparity in non-relativistic and relativistic regimes. The research establishes a relationship between zeta and gamma factors and shows that GUP can lead to the disappearance of relativistic length contraction, while giving rise to a novel mutation effect. Additionally, the study presents a model based on GUP that predicts the mass of the graviton.

Multitasking scheduling in service industries has gained significant attention due to workers frequently transitioning between tasks. Building on the foundation of shared-processing knowledge, this research extends scheduling models to incorporate multitasking workers. We introduce two new parameters: the probability of shared processing and the probability of task overlap. These concepts are initially applied to a single-server queue and later extended to more complex settings with multiple servers. We obtain probabilistic waiting times for customers in the queue and analyze the performance of two scheduling strategies under preemptive and non-preemptive scenarios. Numerical examples illustrate the impact of various parameters on system performance.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when interacting with soft and irregular terrain, causing established control methods to fall short. These challenges are particularly highlighted in tasks requiring rapid hopping, such as navigating dense forests and uneven terrain, where traditional controllers fail to adapt. To address these difficulties, this study aims to develop an integrated framework for legged locomotion that accounts for ground behavior and optimizes control strategies to ensure stable and efficient hopping on soft and irregular surfaces. This framework relies on (1) advanced mathematical representations to simulate the interaction between a legged robot and variable terrain, (2) an optimization technique for creating feasible motion paths, and (3) feedback control using model predictive control, which enables real-time trajectory adjustment. This study utilizes a single hopping robot as a test case and develops an optimization technique for fuel-efficient and rapidly hopping on various ground models. The results from simulations and experiments confirm the effectiveness and accuracy of this framework, demonstrating the potential to improve legged locomotion control, particularly in complex and challenging environments.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are vital for maintaining optimal security and reliability. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via codified policy decisions and exchangeable code (security-as-a-code), these updates should become standard practice. However, deploying firmware updates across vast IoT networks poses a significant challenge, particularly in areas with a large number of constrained wireless devices. In this study, we undertook a large-scale measurement model to analyze how IoT networks respond to shared resources and mesh-like connectivity, focusing on the impact of concurrent update operations. Our investigation, conducted using 1,440 IoT devices in a test mesh network, revealed important insights that can inform system administrators and policymakers, and ultimately enhance the efficiency of firmware update processes across conventional IoT networks.

We employ a recursive Green function approach to obtain the Fock space propagator and associated self-energy for one-dimensional interacting fermions in a disordered system. Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary component, which governs the decay rate of initial states, exhibits a distinct transition across the many-body localization point, aligning with theoretical predictions. By examining the probability of initial states surviving this decay, we establish a fractal dimension that accounts for the diversity in state persistence rates across the disorder spectrum. This dimensionful quantity not only characterizes the complexity of states before the many-body localization point but also displays a singular behavior at the critical point, as well as an extensive increase in diversity dimensions beyond it, with the latter's values conforming to a classification system based on topological invariants derived from a theory involving phase transitions driven by chaos.

To make the most out of human insight, interactive graph label propagation combines artificial intelligence with human intelligence. However, current methods fall short by focusing on finding a single solution at a time, which doesn't efficiently utilize human expertise. In this research, we tackle the challenge of simultaneously identifying multiple targets within a graph by utilizing insights from an expert. We propose the concept of a stowaway to represent possible label combinations for each target, creating a condensed and interconnected graph where solutions can interplay and impact one another. A novel algorithm is introduced, which selects the most promising stowables after each round of inquiry, leading to improved target identification at a lower cost. In comparison to existing methods, our findings demonstrate that this multiple-target approach yields more accurate results while requiring significantly fewer queries.

The exploration of quantum machine learning has demonstrated the potential for
groundbreaking insights in both areas of research. Experimental findings indicate
that quantum computers could significantly outperform traditional machines in
certain machine learning tasks, although they may also be susceptible to
adversarial threats. These threats involve introducing small, manipulative
distortions to legitimate data that cause high-performing quantum and
conventional machines to make inaccurate predictions. Our study marks the first
time that universal adversarial examples have been identified for both quantum and
conventional machines using real-world data. Furthermore, we discovered
adversarial examples and perturbations that could be applied simultaneously to
both types of machines to accurately predict a given dataset. Our research
investigated the applications of quantum neural networks, specifically two
quantum-inspired machines, to understand the differences in their
vulnerabilities. Our findings pave the way for future research on quantum
machine learning robustness.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues for almost-spherical domains in the class D_ω. We establish that for domains in the D_ω class with small symmetry breaking, each Steklov eigenvalue can be expressed as a series of Wigner-Eisenberg phases, associated with rotations of almost-spherical domains, to second-order accuracy. This finding aligns with numerical findings reported in [M. Gamba, S. Mazzucato, J. Ralston, J. Roppo, J. Compy. Dyn., 2018]. Furthermore, we prove that for domains in the D_ω class, each Steklov eigenvalue corresponds to a homotopy class of maps from the rotation group SO(2) to the 1-dimensional sphere.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data.

Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models, although computationally simple, are often inaccurate due to oversimplifications in their statistical basis. In contrast, deterministic models, like those based on ray tracing and physical wave propagation laws, provide precise predictions but require significant computational resources and can only utilize traditional geographical data. In this article, a groundbreaking approach to radio propagation modeling using deep neural networks is presented. By leveraging spatially indexed data, these all-terrain deep learning-based propagation models are adaptable, precise, and efficient to compute. Furthermore, they can also predict wave forms and channel impulse response for various wireless communications applications. We develop and visually demonstrate two neural network architectures, DCP-M and DCP-S, that predict mean and spatial standard deviation of path loss, facilitating the generation of spatial distributions of signal strength. Our study includes a thorough analysis of DCP-M/DCP-S architecture, training procedure, and an examination of its performance in real-world scenarios with respect to other widely used propagation models. All related source code and data can be found on https://github.com/pannenkoek777/Deep-Propagation.

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then obtain a validation algorithm based on that semantics. By using a formal Isabelle/HOL proof, it is shown that the validation algorithm faithfully represents the developed semantics. We also demonstrate through practical experiments that the verification of our algorithm is useful.

Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Through case studies involving capital costs, varied weather conditions, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate the method's value and reveal that models are most susceptible to temporal resolution. Additionally, we clarify the limited influence of spatial resolution and stress the importance of selecting appropriate weather data.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation.

When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely written requests for change, described using everyday language and involving relevant technical terms. The task requires identifying key terms related to the request's technical context, allowing developers to refine their search and locate relevant sections in the software code. Existing approaches to this challenge have been somewhat effective, though they still struggle with understanding natural language at a satisfactory level. The proposed system, STRICT, takes a different approach, taking the change request itself as its primary source of information. By taking this request as its starting point, STRICT identifies key terms relevant to the request, while conventional methods rely on less informative initial requests. The system was tested on a dataset combining requests from two open-source projects, comparing its performance to existing state-of-the-art methods. The results indicate that STRICT outperforms these methods, successfully pinpointing key terms in a given request with greater precision.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which can be measured with precision, can occur at sound levels as mild as those encountered in everyday environments. Moreover, the introduction of ultrasonic vibrations significantly softens the gel's structure, enhances its ability to flow, and even alters the size of its particles. Our findings suggest that ultrasonic gel modifications can last beyond the duration of the vibration and that this technique may be used to improve the process of loading and unloading particles into colloidal gels. Researchers have also proposed a complex model explaining how ultrasonic gel behavior works. This model will serve as a foundation for future studies on these materials, paving the way for the potential application of ultrasonic technology in transporting particles through gels in the future.

This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is then generalized to encompass all positive odd integers. By applying the principle of mathematical induction, this extended set is used to prove the conjecture. A second verification of the conjecture via mathematical induction is also presented in section 9. In addition, the paper calculates the Lyapunov time for a specific case of the Collatz iteration. The Lyapunov time serves as a measure of the stability of the Collatz iterative process. The paper's ultimate goal is to resolve the long-standing puzzle associated with the Collatz conjecture through in-depth analysis.

To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a specific field, precise categorization of document subjects is crucial in various areas of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Currently, most subject classification methods rely on human expertise, but automated approaches using machine learning have shown promising results, despite the challenge of communicating classification decisions in an easily understandable manner. In this study, we focus on addressing this challenge by combining existing STEM subject classification with mathematical entity monitoring to explain the classification of a document with a simple, intuitive story. Our proposed approach involves a novel method for linking mathematical entities in an extensive collection, and we demonstrate its application in creating personalized, human-like explanations for classification subjects. Given the current limitations of existing STEM subject classification datasets, we created a new, combined dataset in the field of STEM subject classification and mathematical entity monitoring, and the resulting classifications were enhanced by the MEL method with explanations that significantly exceeded human written levels of detail. Our research suggests that explanations of STEM subject classifications can be intriguingly imaginative and mathematically rich, and the resulting benefit in terms of what can be learned from the data far exceeds traditional machine learning approaches.

To guarantee matching among all agents, the Deferred Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, research suggests that preferences are not always expressed uniformly across different contexts, and, in fact, the majority rule often leads to unstable matches when preferences are divided into strong and weak opinions. In response, we introduce a new model where agents prioritize their strong preferences and make proposals accordingly, only converting to their secondary preferences if initial attempts fail. Through an analysis within the framework of graph invariants and case studies, our investigation aims to explore the capabilities and limitations of this proposed model. We demonstrate that when all agents are capable of making the same number of proposals, the resulting matches are guaranteed to be stable and achieve optimal social welfare when preferences are essentially pairwise in nature.
