Here, it's demonstrated that even in the absence of a solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm still converges to a seismic coupling that best approximates the reference coupling. Furthermore, a specific condition is provided to determine which metric coupling serves as the limit of the algorithm. Our results were initially presented at the 31st French Conference on Probability and Statistics.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data in 2018 in both proton-proton and proton-lead collision modes, resulting in measurements of the top-quark pair cross-section in the proton-proton mode at a 5.02 TeV center-of-mass energy. The proton-lead mode's data, published elsewhere, allowed a determination of the nuclear modification factor for the top-quark pair's cross-section in the leading proton's rapidity range. The proton-proton data's measurement serves as a reference point for these studies. The cross-section measurement leverages 2018's high-luminosity ATLAS dataset and a selection of 36.7 fb^-1, relying on a simplified template reconstruction of the top-quark pairs and incorporating events featuring one accepted $W$ or $Z$ boson. The cross-section was determined from the fully hadronic decays of both $W$ and $Z$ bosons and adjacent $j$ jets to be 342.7 ± 2.7 (statistical) ± 4.6 (systematic) ± 3.6 (luminosity) ± 5.4 (beam energy) ± 2.5 (data release variation) ± 0.4 (electroweak) pb. The calculated value deviates from theoretical estimates only by 8% with the top-quark pairs' fixed next-to-leading order matrix element and matrix elements and parton showers generating the hadronic

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would influence the behavior of its core element. Researchers have recently investigated the impact of this phenomenon in the context of systems involving multiple interacting particles coupled with a central qubit or cavity, which are referred to as Hub-and-Spoke (H&S) systems. These studies have shown that the core element exhibits unique characteristics under specific conditions and make remarkable predictions about its future behavior. Specifically, our work focuses on the electromagnetic interaction between atomic constituents of a molecule and a central superconducting qubit, which enables us to accurately forecast localization dynamics. Conversely, when utilizing a central optical cavity coupled with highly interacting, multiple-component particles in the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard (JCH) model, our results show that the cavity's three-level Dicke state exhibits unique localization properties that depend on certain critical thresholds. These findings emphasize the importance of considering the specific characteristics of both the core element and the surrounding system or environment when studying the behavior of these complex systems.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified such that 
the series $e_m(z)$, where $m > 0$, involves complex parameters and 
maps the unit disk to the exterior of an ellipse in the complex plane, 
resulting in a conformal, univalent mapping. This leads to a solution for 
the extended Riemann mapping problem. Furthermore, this solution is applied 
to categorize generalized Bessel functions within the Janowski class.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health in a way that balances strict measures with maintaining social benefits for years to come.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising sequential or additive multigrid strategies to accelerate
the computational speed of complex two-phase flow problems within diverse porous
media. We introduce a pioneering nonlinear preconditioner in the context of control
volume distributed systems. We integrate our preconditioner into advanced nonlinear
preconditioner combinations, such as SMES and SMPS, and comparative evaluations
are conducted with prevalent preconditioner variants, specifically the linear field
split-preconditioner and a nonlinear preconditioner known as the pressure-temperature
preconditioner, within esteemed third-order element-based simulations of steam
injection for geothermal power at multiple scales. We also conduct thorough
experiments on smaller-scale problems with randomly generated media to thoroughly
understand the strengths and limitations of our proposed preconditioner. Our
investigation's outcomes showcase the proposed preconditioner's exceptional
performance, robustness, flexibility, and scalability in both theoretical studies and
real-world applications.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for efficient interactions between light and the chiral entity. A scenario exists where circularly polarized light can be confined within a cavity formed by mirrors with uniform, yet optically active surface reflections. This is achievable in a novel type of optical cavity comprising 2 circularly polarized mirrors that interact with a chiral medium, as a result of the combination of conventional reflection and medium-induced polarization shifts. This chiral cavity can't be characterized by the conventional parameters that describe non-chiral cavities. However, using advanced mathematical techniques, researchers have managed to derive full building instructions for constructing the "mirror" surface components in both homogeneous and periodic arrangements of different materials. Upon realization, the proposed chiral optical cavity is expected to provide unprecedented levels of extremely intense, localized magnetic and electric field regions. These intense field regions could be utilized for specialized applications, including highly accurate inspections of material properties, stimulation of specific chemical reactions or physical properties within chiral substances, as well as efficient data transfer through the chiral property of transverse polarization polarization when paired with circular propagation.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on a space with two dimensions and a non-rigorous, c=0 string theory, specifically focusing on Liouville conformal field theory. We start with a observation about the Seiberg bound, then derive three key points: one regarding the spectrum of Liouville theory, another about the boundary of the Szekeres' solution in the context of JT gravity, and finally regarding the duality between JT gravity and a simple matrix model. We also provide a alternative, rigorous formulation of this matrix model.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This research extends our previous solutions by applying the Einstein equations to the warp drive metric, incorporating both a perfect fluid source and a perfect fluid source with a perfect fluid energy-momentum inhomogeneous distribution, including a term for vacuum polarization, in models that exhibit symmetry with the x-y, x-z, and y-z planes. In all of these solutions, the warp drive region is modeled as a perfect fluid with negative pressure, and we find that introducing a perfect fluid with positive pressure in the exterior region does not significantly affect the warp drive metrics in the interior region. Nevertheless, incorporating a term for vacuum polarization in these solutions results in the greatest reduction in the minimum amount of negative energy density required for warp drive to be achievable.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, acquiring data, and tracking costs while lacking the support of modern urban management systems. In response, cities turn to technology solutions, although many existing platforms isolate specific infrastructure types or focus on a single application, failing to address the complexities of integrated city planning. Furthermore, the shift towards digitized city infrastructure creates a vast potential for analytical insights on urban functions, but cities are held back due to technical limitations and fragmented approaches. The Guides project addresses these challenges by developing engineering solutions for digitized city infrastructure data through the creation of a flexible, urban information model that can incorporate various infrastructure types and support multiple use cases across urban platforms.

To analyze dephasing from spin fluctuations, we developed and employed a method to analyze the fluctuations in population of the M=1, -1 states as a function of total magnetic field. This method has high precision due to the long trapping time for our calcium ions. The results show that the temperature of the ion string in equilibrium matches the lattice temperature. The probability distribution of excited states follows a Gaussian with minimal fluctuations. The main source of vibrational energy excitation in our system is photoexcitation of the ions. The temperature of the string after the mystery mode is around 20(1) microK, but this rises to around 40 microK after the mystery mode is excited. The mystery mode's temperature is around 6 microK. The mystery mode is found to be activated by the A1 mode during the Raman rotation and also possibly exists in neighboring crystal configurations.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines the primary factors driving the effectiveness of TERS, the electromagnetic and chemical interactions, into a single quantum simulation. The electromagnetic influence describes the sample's interaction with highly localized, inhomogeneous electric fields produced by the plasmonic tip. On the other hand, the chemical interaction accounts for the distinct responses between the apex tip and sample constituents. Our algorithm uses wave functions from a basis set to calculate plasmon modes and couple them with sample dipoles, thus enabling the calculation of localized fields. By cross-correlating these dipoles and fields, we can generate, for the first time, chemically informative second harmonic generation (SHG) signals. Our research indicates that the chemical effect is more critical in TERS than previously thought and is the dominant contributor to chemical images. Additionally, the electromagnetic effect is a crucial factor in determining the intensity of the SHG signals. Our simulations provide detailed explanations for a range of TERS phenomena, starting from basic chemical effects to the presence of plasmon resonances, light polarization, and sample layering. Our study offers the first ab initio, theoretically grounded description of TERS, a technique with vast applications, and highlights the necessity for considering both the electromagnetic and chemical impacts in the system.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular attention to how their emission relates to M 31. Through radio-continuum data and global photometry at 18.6 and 24.6 GHz, we sought to find M31's AME contribution by differentiating its total flux density from that of M33. After processing and analyzing the K band data obtained with the Sardinia Radio Telescope, we determined that the galaxies NGC 3109, NGC 2997, and M33 do not exhibit detectable AME excess beyond 2 sigma. If we assume the M31 flux density at 18.6 GHz is similar to that at 24.6 GHz, we found their total AME contribution could be as high as 5.5 mJy, although this is highly dependent on various factors and indicates the AME is likely an insignificant portion of their total flux density. Our measurements are consistent with the average AME emissions of similar galaxies in our Local Group.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model of entropy involving disorder across the high-symmetry phase's mirror plane, it is now clear that this simplistic model is invalid. Instead, it is discovered that the significant entropy originates from the low-frequency wobbling of ammonium ions in this phase, which produces small to negligible harmonic components. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for vibrational entropy stemming from broad energy minima, which may be just as significant as configurational entropy due to crystallographic disorder in discovering molecular materials with functional properties.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and an interesting aspect is the similarity between this and maximization at a brain level.  We provide evidence that explains a range of behaviors by developing a model.  This model was tested by collecting the data of sixty individuals, which showed that people exhibiting probability-matching are integrating negative outcomes to a higher degree while learning, which means that there's a stronger connection between the midbrain and an error measure.  Moreover, the results showed that an individual's learning style doesn't change over various situations and therefore it can be described as a consistent characteristic.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined. Despite their different complexities, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem Involves Preprocessing a set of curves to enable efficient query lookup for their closest approximate matches within a given radius, with the goal of achieving a time complexity of O(q log^d n / \epsilon) using t inserts per update, where q is the number of queries, d is the dimensionality, n is the number of input curves, and t is the number of updates. Our analysis of the FANNG data structure leads to the first non-trivial worst-case input bounds for this problem, with the following results: For a given set of piecewise linear curves in the plane, we prove that there exists an algorithm supporting t inserts per update with a time complexity of O((q + n) log^2 n / (\epsilon)^2) and showing that this is a tight result for any t > 1. Furthermore, we extend the FANNG analysis to cover piecewise linear and constant step curves in k-dimensional space, resulting in the achievement of comparable bounds for these variants. Our analysis of the FANNG data structure, albeit limited to these variants, underscores the challenge of deriving straightforward, intuitive, and biologically-inspired algorithms for approximate near neighbor problems that yield simple, scalable, and worst-case input bounds.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared autonomy focuses on developing advanced statistical models to identify the task, however these models are often based on historical data and fail when the robot encounters novel circumstances. To overcome this, we suggest that robots adopt a distinct method where they verbally communicate possible task conventions to the human, who then verifies if the perceived tasks align with their intentions. Through an experimental study, we demonstrate that by presenting the human with a limited number of plausible task conventions, collaboration and productivity are significantly enhanced, even when the robot's understanding of the task is inaccurate. This collaborative technique is versatile and can be applied in various scenarios, including visual and haptic interactions. We have developed an open-source system for automatic generation of task conventions and a corresponding simulation environment used in our study.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

Research into two-dimensional arrays of digital sequences driven by digital signals has been a key focus in the field of communications technology, particularly regarding the properties of two-dimensional Z-consultary array sequences. Previous studies were centered on two-dimensional linear shift-invariant arrays, exploring various functions that form multivariable functions to achieve desired properties. However, conventional variable functions used in prior studies are restricted to specific expressions, hindering the direct construction of suitable two-dimensional Z-consultary array sequences. Therefore, this paper addresses this challenge by proposing a novel inter-group complementary code set, enabling the direct construction of 2-D Z-consultary array sequences based on any given multivariable functions.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual-energy technique, which separates materials based on their X-ray absorption patterns, offers valuable insights but also falls short when dealing with noisy data. A significant limitation common to these methods is the requirement for a predetermined number of materials, which may not always be feasible. A proposed variational reconstruction model overcomes these limitations by estimating image patterns, denosing input data, and decomposing materials in an unsupervised manner. The model's performance has been assessed using real-world data sets with the assistance of a specially designed graphics processing unit (GPU), which enabled the efficient recovery of patterns and the unsupervised classification of materials into distinct groups.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local response model that excludes the spillover region from the calculation. This model provides a user-friendly alternative for making predictions about the behavior of metallic structures at the quantum level without the computational intricacies associated with quantum electrodynamics.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that enhanced results can be achieved when users also specify the relative significance of those terms. Although CNER bears some resemblance to related concepts such as List Question answering and Entity disambiguation, its primary goal is to gather user feedback to dynamically construct a class of entity profiles and leverage this data for extracting entities from unrestricted text. Our focus in CNER involves identifying relevant sentences containing entities similar to a selected query entity. This paper presents a new technique, using human-relevant term context to identify analogous sentences. Our framework combines this context with a contextual distance metric, which measures the similarity between the query entity and retrieved context sentences. As the concept of context is quite abstract, support is provided in the form of a tool to guide users and illustrate CNER and its sub-components. Our approach achieves a 22% boost in average precision over the best-existing Baseline and surpasses the current CNER benchmark of 52% in a 10-shot setting.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its analysis. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we need to analyze how different components evolve over time. Our approach focuses on uncovering patterns within this evolving data, and we must efficiently communicate our findings to others, particularly when dealing with large amounts of informative data. Standard interactive visualizations, such as scatter plots and those offering linked views, become difficult to use when dealing with complex data sets. Our solution involves creating an interactive wall display that utilizes an animated surface, showing the development of longitudinal patterns and enabling the exploration of complex data in a more accessible way. Our approach centers on uncovering patterns in the data, and we must efficiently analyze and communicate our findings to others. Our method uses the "inspector" – a movable window within the wall display – to offer an in-depth examination of any section of the wall, revealing detailed information on time-based patterns. Our approach allows users to date, category, or randomly explore sections of the wall, and our method uses the "inspector” to offer in-depth examination, and our results show the efficacy of this method in facilitating exploration and offering insights to analysts conducting their investigations.

The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall healthcare quality. Advances in recent years have seen the development of sequential or graph-based models aiming to tackle this goal. Despite the complexity and diversity of EHR data, which can be visualized as a multi-layered network (heterogeneous), existing studies have neglected the rich structural information contained within it. Moreover, the clinical relationships bringing meaning to these documents have not been adequately captured. Our proposed Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN) aims to overcome these shortcomings by incorporating graph neural networks to analyze diverse EHR representations and their structural associations. This innovative framework incorporates knowledge graph learning to discover latent clinical relations and enable efficient similarity computations between various EHR components. Our experiments demonstrate the substantial superiority of HSGNN over existing baselines across diverse problem settings, as evidenced by the results of MIMIC-III and ICU clinical risk prediction tasks.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. Based on a modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation, we derive analytical solutions for a planar interface and numerical results for a cylindrical and spherical geometry. Accounting for the distribution of charged particles away from the flexible material's surface, we consider the impact of solvent polarization on the electrostatic properties of the flexible material. Our study shows that solvent polarization significantly affects the distribution of ions near the surface of the flexible material. As a result, the capacitance of the electric double layer and the pressure on the material's surface change in response to the material's charge density, size, and the concentration of the surrounding electrolyte. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions under which the capacitance per area exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the size of the flexible material. Our findings provide valuable insights into the electrostatic properties of the material, essential for understanding the behavior of the material in various biological, chemical, and technological processes.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with well-established models like fastText and ELMo. To challenge the model with more complex text, we compared PURE's performance with experiments conducted on less formal Request For Information (RFI) documents. The fine-tuned BERT model achieved encouraging results on the PURE dataset, demonstrating superior performance on binary sentence classification with a high level of confidence for both exact and fuzzy matching texts. However, the model's accuracy declined when classifying sentences with less formal language in RFI documents. Although BERT shows promise for automated requirement extraction, it is clear that there are significant hurdles to overcome for this complex task.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a limited number of relays available to assist the transmitter in reducing interference and increasing spectral efficiency through network coding techniques. To optimize energy consumption and reliability, the problem is framed as a joint optimization task involving relay selection and transmitter power allocation, solved using a low-complexity algorithm that utilizes a mixed-integer programming method. A cooperative diversity gain measure is introduced to evaluate system performance and reliability, represented as the proportion of selected relays to the total number available. Our results demonstrate that the proposed strategy achieves full diversity gain when all relays are selected and ensures a balance between diversity gain and energy efficiency. Furthermore, the study examines how to maximize energy efficiency under fixed relay selection, formulating this problem as a convex optimization task and solving it using a quadratic approximation technique. Simulation outcomes confirm the efficacy of the proposed strategy in achieving optimal energy efficiency while maintaining reliable communication.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local density of states (LDOS). Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms, Mn dimers on a superconducting Nb(110) surface were conducted. These calculations suggested the emergence of novel YSR states within the superconducting gap, as well as the creation of YSR states crossing the Fermi level within specific energy ranges. Furthermore, analyses indicated that certain YSR states could be prone to pairing instability. Initially, the theoretical framework was trained using data from an Mn adatom on a semi-infinite Nb(110) surface to establish material-specific parameters. Subsequently, the established model was used to analyze Mn dimers separated by one or seven lattice constants. Our findings proposed the feasibility of distinguishing between different competitive ordering scenarios of the YSR states for non-equivalent impurities. Additionally, the theoretical framework enabled the prediction of quantum fluctuations associated with YSR states with a zero-temperature binding energy.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Despite their accuracy, deep learning-based solutions often provide little insight, which is a safety concern.  To bridge this gap, our paper introduces an approach that involves selectively removing portions of the point cloud with inconsistencies, using local network estimates to identify potential registration errors and suppress points that disagree with point cloud transforms in those areas, leading to improved registration results, with significant accuracy benefits for scenes featuring dense foliage and other challenges to traditional methods.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure and large volumes of annotated data. In 
the context of massive satellite datasets, securing sufficient computational 
resources and annotated data can become financially and logistically burdensome.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a distinct absorption spectrum, known as a non-linear XANES (NEXAFS) spectrum, which records the material's state during near-linear electronic confinement. The notion that electronic temperatures provide a comprehensive understanding of these dynamics is insufficient, leading to the development of a unified theoretical model that describes the dynamic evolution of the material's electronic population and associated distribution across a set of initial and final bound states. The proposed model, grounded in a quantum mechanical framework, identifies several distinct eras of excitation, including a initial era characterized by core-excited states whose statistical distribution across initial states determines the final NEXAFS spectrum. The model also recognizes a era of rapid core-excitation during which the excitation of valence-band states supplies energy to the core-excited states. Mathematical equations from this era demonstrate the substantial influence of initial and final states on the final NEXFAS spectrum, revealing the role of final states to be independent of fluence, in contrast to initial states. The model includes a new parameter denoted as the shell overlap factor (SOCF) that reflects the spatial proximity of initial and final states involved in a transition, illustrating its effects on

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks by removing malicious interference before feeding data into a DNN-based classifier. The proposed approach specifically protects AMC systems from attacks like the Fast-Gradient Sign method. The existing GAN countermeasures were ineffective in our scenario, so we employed a new variant that uses multiple generators to avoid a mode collapsing issue common in radio signal classification. Simulation results indicate that this countermeasure can improve the DNN-based AMC's accuracy against attacks by 81% in our test cases.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques but most
methods are one-dimensional as they rely on a single, pre-prepared dataset.
In contrast, a new approach presents the "AutoSeg" task as a series of
sequential learning exercises, allowing the incorporation of datasets from multiple
hospitals sequentially.  The study employed a state-of-the-art computer vision
technique, training it to accurately identify lesions from new, previously unseen
datasets continuously.  Even with the added complexity of interpreting clinical
examinations and understanding disease states, the model demonstrated high
accuracy in lesion segmentation.  Moreover, the study demonstrated that this
new approach achieved comparable accuracy to traditional methods, while using
significantly fewer resources.  The study's findings are available online for
free at: https://github.com/multpleScleroses/learn-continally-SMSeg

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a notion of continuity.

Across various disciplines, there's considerable interest in creating predictive models for how intricate systems with many interacting components evolve over time. In the context of classical statistics, researchers have developed accurate predictive models based on data from similar systems. Recently, there has been an emphasis on adapting these methods to make predictions about unfamiliar or partially observed systems. In this study, a statistical framework for developing predictive models has been established, with simulations demonstrating improved accuracy compared to traditional approaches. The new framework is seen as a significant step towards creating universal models that can make predictions with more certainty.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, and this mass disparity cannot be explained by the initial mass function when considering the cores' potential for future star formation. This suggests cores undergo mass growth during the earliest stages of their formation.  The extent of core mass growth varies, and it significantly correlates with the initial core mass, hinting that larger cores have the potential to give rise to the most massive stars.  For the purposes of these calculations, it has been assumed that core mass dispersion among embedded cores reflects their initial distribution pre-outflow emergence.  In light of these findings, it is the hypothesis that this mass growth phase, characteristic of core evolution, extends to the most massive forms of formative cores, namely supercritical ridges.  The implications of these discoveries for star formation theories and the predicted initial mass functions are substantial, and they are expected to be even more pronounced at higher mass extremes.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational interactions. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study these interactions and predict the likelihood of certain observations. To better understand the predictions of this model, we used PopSyCLE to generate 1000 random realizations of primordial black holes and their effects on the universe, considering different scenarios. Our analysis of these scenarios suggests that, given the right conditions, primordial black holes could potentially explain the observed universe darkness and account for the various star formations across different star types. Our study provides a foundation for future research into the relationship between stars and primordial black holes, offering new insights into the nature of dark matter.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the system's behavior being controlled solely by the entropy of molecular arrangement. For systems where the packing density was below $0.5$, in addition to the standard liquid state, we observed standard nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. This was confirmed by analyzing order parameters. Conversely, when the packing density exceeded $0.5$, two distinct crystalline phases emerged alongside a typical kinetic proof of crystal lattice ordering, characterized by the presence of defects. Specifically, in the high-density crystalline phase, the lattice was found to be hexagonal with vertical ordering of molecules through the centers of the largest spheres, characterized by a specific helical structure; this was distinct from the low-density crystalline phase, which exhibited a specific helical structure within certain molecular layers.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the token embeddings and linear projections for classification tasks.
By introducing unique special tokens for each dataset, their corresponding embeddings and linear projections are fine-tuned during the tuning process, and these special tokens are added to the input sequence. Several strategies are examined to optimize performance, including pre-training the special tokens through data sampling, utilizing common data across multiple tasks, and selecting a strategy to handle datasets with limited samples. The results show that PASTA consistently achieves performance at par with or superior to PLOUT, the current state-of-the-art parameter-efficient tuning method, and yields substantial updates to model parameters while also providing a notable speedup in training times.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-based preference modeling. We examine two distinct models – the Kullback-Leibler and the Jeffreys divergences – to compare their performance in ranking sets of different sizes. While the J-divergence offers several advantages, including the ability to discard the null set and an intuitive parameter interpretation, our empirical analysis reveals that the Kullback-Leibler divergence provides better asymptotic performance. Nonetheless, the J-divergence remains a valuable option due to its robustness in large sample scenarios and its capability to regulate the impact of contextual information.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interconnected thermodynamic properties as supported by recent experimental data from Caruthers and Medvedev. This relationship enables us to reframe the generalized entropy theory for glass formation and relaxation, relating energy and configurational entropy to predict relaxation behaviors. Specifically, we use this approach to explain the diverse aging phenomena in simple polymers and how they conform to the universal thermal glass transition scenario. We also contrast our theoretical findings with those from simple liquids based on experimental data from binary and multi-component polymers, presenting opportunities for future research.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to process these negation types. Our analysis indicates models perform notably well on some negation categories, revealing a significant distinction in their handling of this concept.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models with non-polynomial potential functions in odd dimensional spaces, leading to a new class of interacting conformal field theories. Specifically, this results in CFTs for dimensions 3+4n where n is a positive integer. Calculations of thermal entropy are also carried out for these same dimensions and time periods, revealing a relationship between the entropy rates and entanglement entropy in the large N limit. Interestingly, this relationship holds only if the potential function meets a specific non-constant condition for certain ranges of couplings in 3+4n dimensions. However, this condition is not met in 5d. Additionally, this research suggests that there might be a phase transition in 5d without a gap in the spectrum, where this could be verified by analyzing the spectrum under a specific large N limit condition, though this is still purely speculative.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior theorem by Cai et al. and confirming a previously suspected truth. Moreover, we expand upon their work by including subcase (iii) with a general diffusion model. Specifically, we utilize the CTMC framework to calculate the Laplace transforms of two popular models: the general arithmetic-geometric Asian option and the mixed diffusion model. Notably, we enhance the existing findings for the general arithmetic-geometric model and provide new results for the mixed diffusion model.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and cosmic clusters may all play a part in this phenomenon. Researchers conducted a study that simulated how cosmic rays interact within galactic clusters using cosmological magnetohydrodynamical models. Their analysis, spanning a range of redshifts, suggests that cosmic ray interactions with magnetic fields in galactic clusters could account for up to 100% of the gamma-ray flux measured by Fermi-LAT within the energy range of 100 MeV to 100 GeV. Building upon this discovery, researchers have created predictive models that correlate the gamma-ray intensity with the count of cosmic clusters within a particular horizon. Their forecasts also anticipate that future observational tools like HAWC and CTA will be able to detect the gamma-ray intensity emitted by cosmic clusters, thereby shedding light on the mysterious diffuse gamma-ray background.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can lead to the non-zero kinetic energy of produced particles at early times, reversing the usual suppression and facilitation the detection of quantum effects in late universe. Our findings reveal that primordial features can pave a viable pathway for investigating quantum effects in inflationary universe, thus providing a promising avenue for the study of quantum collapse.

In this study, we introduce a new technique to analyze convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with the aim of understanding their visual interpretations. Unlike existing methods that create simplified representations by removing key parts of the network or employing approximate algorithms, our proposed filter attention method preserves the network's original structure while using a simplified criterion. The attention model identifies the most important filters and sub-networks within CNNs, enabling us to study how these components contribute to the network's performance. Our experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the attention model in identifying critical filters and pinpointing the specific visual patterns (e.g., body, face, text, etc.) that these filters detect. Moreover, the attention model allows us to train a smaller CNN from pre-existing models by stripping away unessential filters and leveraging the latent sub-networks for new tasks, a technique known as transfer learning. Our findings demonstrate the benefits of this approach, with the newly designed CNN demonstrating superior performance on facial key point detection and image classification tasks.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity. Our research focuses on one-dimensional materials, which are theoretically easier to analyze. We investigated the electronic properties of (Doped) $1T$-TaSe$_2$, a recently discovered one-dimensional system, and found that it exhibits a gapless electronic band due to strong correlations. Furthermore, our study of the uncoded electron-lattice interaction in one-dimensional materials reveals the existence of long-range attractive potentials. These interactions persist in three-dimensional materials lacking inversion symmetry. We propose that phonon-mediated long-range interactions are crucial in driving high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates and other related materials.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the key factors driving the epidemic. This study proposes a novel causal learning approach to identify crucial indicators and causal links related to the 90-90-90 targets. This method preserves critical information about key factors, in contrast to existing approaches which often result in significant data loss. Using a synthetic dataset inspired by the MPHIA survey design and structured in a graph database, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by identifying the primary indicators and causal links in HIV treatment pathways.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, it's discovered that the transition from a metastable skyrmion lattice at room temperature to an equilibrium helical state, when triggered by magnetic fields, goes through a phase characterized by partial topological charge reversal. Utilizing Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, the magnetization patterns within this material were directly visualized while under the influence of external magnetic fields. Upon further investigation, it's found that the metastable skyrmion lattice stage exhibits unique properties: first, skyrmion stabilization occurs at lower magnetic fields than anticipated, indicating enhanced magnetic stability; second, the skyrmion lattice shows reduced topological stability with increasing magnetic fields, eventually transforms into a near-helical state composed of curved and intersecting magnetic strips, demonstrating a nearly complete disappearance of initial topological charge; finally, the transition from the metastable state to a stable helical configuration presents an interesting exception to the theoretical prediction that loses entropy always runs its course.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation of 
these models, focusing specifically on singular ARMA models, is examined. The 
paper prioritizes detailing model types and their underlying structure, 
rather than estimation methodologies, aiming to highlight innovative 
research avenues and applicable areas which are still underdeveloped.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical challenges persist due to signal noise that hinders model performance and the need to approximate the inverse model, despite the incremental progress made. To overcome these obstacles, this research presents an innovative solution by integrating Bayesian neural networks into reversible steganography. The primary contribution of our method lies in the design of a signal noise mitigation strategy that focuses on optimizing the signal, thereby enhancing the predictive model's accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses existing solutions in both quantitative measures and qualitative insights. The corresponding source code can be accessed at https://github.com/sad11223/BNN-RS.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely employed framework to link these effects to fundamental properties of convective dynamos, although its application relies heavily on adjustable parameters. By utilizing self-consistent solutions of inhomogeneous convective dynamos, incorporating full spectra of turbulent effects, we have identified crucial requirements that necessitate re-evaluation of the standard framework. The significance of turbulent effects in the Sun and early stars/planets demands a deeper understanding of these requirements.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected four distinct plumes of molecular gas, possibly corresponding to gas situated at the edges of an existing ionized outflow. It has been observed that the molecular gas in NGC4945 is oriented perpendicularly to the galaxy's major axis. An outflow model consistent with stellar mass has been developed using the velocity of the molecular gas. It is proposed that the galaxy's outflow is likely caused by an interaction between the galaxy's supermassive black hole and the surrounding material. However, it is also possible that the outflow could be the result of the supermassive black hole's influence on a larger, more complex outflow system common in star-forming galaxies. The outflow was found to be complex and likely not a uniform flow. The observations using the ALMA suggest the gallery ring may be rotating around the supermassive black hole. The observations also reveal a larger, more complex outflow existing beyond 400pc of the galaxy's center. The outflow was found to be 700pc in diameter and has a total mass of 6.8*10^7 M. It also has a total kinetic energy of 1.4*10^57 erg. The flow can be maintained at an estimated rate of 0.02 M. yr^-1. The energy required to create

A simplified version of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations for magnetized plasmas is provided by quasilinear theory, describing how particles interact with waves through resonant processes. The simplified model in a turbulent plasma environment reduces to a complex stochastic differential equation for the distribution of particles, which can be approximated by a partial differential equation assuming a smooth and gradual change in the resulting particle distribution. The assumption leads to a model that overestimates the growth rate of waves when there are discontinuities or sharp changes in the particle distribution. To address this issue, we have developed a numerical solver based on an implicit Galerkin formulation that maintains the accuracy of the required properties of the solution, such as positivity and normalisability. The solver achieves this by enforcing necessary constraints on the solution, ensuring its positivity and smoothness. The solver has been successfully tested on various test cases, including test waves and a simulation of electron heating, demonstrating its ability to preserve these essential properties. The results show good agreement with previous simulations when the properties are preserved, while significant errors occur when the properties are not maintained.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the strong sectoriality of the operator A: X → X*, which also equals the domain of the generator of T.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and web-based tool for determining the interaction cross sections between dimuonium (true muonium) and matter, also computing corresponding form factors. With MuMuPy, users can estimate the likelihood of dimuonium transitioning within an atomic nucleus' electric field. Developed with the muon-based muon-muon electron-positron collider, the muon-muon electron collider, a low-energy electron collider, project proposed by our institute, the Institute of Nuclear Physics at the Budker Institute. We tested the reliability of MuMuPy using three separate methods, including one of which we previously created.

Portfolio managers make investment decisions based on how portfolio performances measure up against the market average or an individual benchmark. The Merton problem offers a theoretical framework for this type of decision-making, where the portfolio manager's gains are evaluated in relation to the market as a whole or an individual asset. The classical Merton problem assumes that the portfolio manager is satisfied if their returns compare favorably to the market, whereas a modified version considers satisfaction as relative to a fixed asset. Both scenarios asset-portfolio dynamics exhibit similar nonlinear characteristics, resulting in an optimal solution obtainable through a closed-form expression under a specific type of utility function. The practical applicability of this solution, however, depends on whether the underlying dynamical system can be easily stabilized or controlled. The analysis focuses on identifying optimal portfolios and discusses the challenges associated with them.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This article centers on the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within dwarf galaxies containing notable quantities of gas and dust. The discussion includes the characteristics of neutral and ionized gases, the effects of dust, and initial evidence suggesting the presence of active nuclei in these galaxies. The article also considers the cosmological implications of primordial helium abundance and the similarity between the interstellar material in companions within pairs/binary systems and the corresponding values in the Milky Way.

We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson model based on a Bethe lattice, where fermions interact with local bosons through a Peierls coupling. By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we demonstrate that despite the presence of multiple bosonic excitations costing zero energy, the quasiparticle is resistant to collapse. The instability of the quasiparticle is heightened under the conditions: (i) an increase in the total number of bosonic excitations costing zero energy and (ii) an increase in the interaction strength between bosons and fermions. This model, which is applicable to other areas, may be particularly useful for analyzing systems featuring the insertion of fermions into domains exhibiting antiferromagnetic or antiferro-orbital ordering that are enclosed by regions of ferromagnetic or ferro-orbital ordering. The described phenomenon could potentially manifest in the underdoped phases of high-temperature superconductors featuring antiferromagnetic ordering. The methods employed in this work could also be used for investigating other models featuring the interaction between fermions and bosons.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3978542} showed that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit linear divergence. The present work extends this analysis to broader classes of these groups. Specifically, we investigate the Brown-Thompson groups $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$ and discover that they too have a linear divergence property. Furthermore, our research encompasses the braided Thompson groups $BF$, $\widehat{BF}$, and $\widehat{BV}$. Alongside existing results in \cite{Kodama:2020to}, our findings confirm that these braided groups display linear divergence as well.

This paper presents a simplified, efficient multi-stage approach to generating responses to questions using the Reformer-based Aggregator with Graph (RAG) architecture. In our method, we initially employ a pre-trained document retriever to identify relevant information from a given dataset. Subsequently, we apply the graph aggregator to the selected documents and refine the entire RAG architecture through multiple iterations of end-to-end fine-tuning, utilizing answers provided in the dataset as training data. This technique achieves exceptional results on the WikiQA dataset, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art outcomes without requiring any pre-processing or specialized models for information extraction. Our results also indicate that the graph aggregator is highly resilient and can produce effective results when the quantity of relevant documents retrieved is substantially lower than in the original RAG pipeline.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in an unconventional manner since no solution to the related problem near the singular point at $x=1$ exists in the current mathematical literature.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a rigorous evaluation pipeline, we demonstrate the ability to exclude unskilled workers before evaluation tasks are initiated, and subsequently collect reliable annotations while maintaining efficient resource allocation. The proposed approach serves as a model for selecting qualified annotators in other complex annotation endeavors.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting nuanced spatial-temporal video representations being a major research priority. Current state-of-the-art models for text-video retrieval primarily utilize pre-trained vision backbones with rigid network architectures, thereby hindering the ability to further refine the video representation and yielding suboptimal results. To overcome this limitation, we present TS2-Net, a groundbreaking transformer architecture incorporating dynamic token shifting and selection, which effectively tailors token sequences to capture the intricate movements in videos and pinpoint critical spatial and temporal details. The TS2-Net's adaptability in shifting token features across frames preserves comprehensive token information, and its token selection mechanism efficiently isolates relevant tokens from input videos. Thorough experiments conducted on multiple benchmark datasets confirm the superior performance of TS2-Net over existing retrieval models.

We've found that neutral flavour-changing currents in top sector physics, linked to electroweak scale particles that interact with leptons, can appear naturally in new physics scenarios, especially in composite Higgs theories. It's been shown that a specific one-loop process, involving a single extra particle beyond the Standard Model and involving a top quark, an electron, and a neutrino, places a limit on how large a flavour-changing coupling can be, given that we've seen no sign of it experimentally yet. This same study has predicted the possible range of couplings for other similar processes, including those involving electrons and tau particles. Another type of process, involving three top quarks and inversely proportional to the square of a flavour-changing coupling, also has theoretical predictions based on how it behaves in different types of new physics scenarios. It's been observed that, in the context of these new physics scenarios (except the standard model itself), except for specific types of new physics scenarios, this cross section generally falls within the range that's consistent with what we currently know about physics.

In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment. This hybrid network is characterized by a configuration ratio that regulates the prevalence of uniform attachment, allowing for more flexibility in its growth compared to purely preferential attachment networks. Two hybrid networks involving directed and undirected link formation are created using a hybrid rule that combines preferential attachment and uniform attachment, leveraging probability ratios to control the likelihood of each type of attachment. Analytical findings regarding the degree distribution, average in-degree, and in-degrees of individual nodes in these hybrid networks match simulations, indicating their validity. These hybrid networks offer potential applications in scenarios where networks require more flexibility and are particularly useful for their undirected variant in modeling networks with weak attachment mechanisms.

The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates dependable interference management systems and hence reliable identification of wireless interference (WII). Our research proposes a novel WII technique that uses a deep convolutional neural network to accurately identify multiple co-channel interference (MCI) sources. The technique is based on a vast dataset of signals collected from various wireless devices, and it effectively detects up to five simultaneous interference sources. The results of our evaluations indicate that our WII approach has a high success rate, and it outperforms traditional methods when classifying interference patterns. The technique is also adaptable to identify device locations or use directional antennas to minimize interference by pinpointing the source and avoiding it.

To grasp the impact of gravitational forces on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and stationary systems, we must integrate quantum mechanics into both general relativity and the cosmic string model. This study analyzes how energy interacts with vorticity, charge, and spin within a gravitational framework, specifically in a state where spatial displacement occurs. We have developed a comprehensive solution for a Klein-Gordon particle in a gravitational field with a cosmic string, considering a particle in motion and a static particle, to gauge the influence of gravitational forces on quantum systems. We have also calculated correlations between the energies of various particle properties under spatial displacement conditions.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton can be understood by analyzing specific interactions between a proton and a photon, specifically in a process known as leptoproduction. Researchers focus on the Compton scattering part of this interaction, which at a certain level can be defined using mathematical integrals involving the parton distributions {H, E, ~H, ~E}.  To date, the distribution 'E' has been difficult to measure since analyzing it requires studying the movement of the proton's neutron, which is impractical. However, theorists have proposed a new method to analyze the differential photon recoil distributions, which could lead to the measurement of the previously hard-to-grasp twist-3 distribution 'E'. By utilizing polarized protons and adjusting their spin orientation, researchers may be able to distinguish between the twist-3 distributions 'E' and ~E'. As a result, the proposed method offers a groundbreaking way to analyze a new discriminative DVCS observable, namely the analysis of the recoil proton polarization.

All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability and distinctness from human errors. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This report outlines an innovative approach aimed at boosting the cognitive capabilities of individual AI systems by collaborating with other AIs. It synthesizes insights from multi-agent learning systems and introduces novel mathematical techniques for non-recursive corrections of legacy AI errors. This study develops a foundational framework for non-destructive AI corrections and derives a sequence of probabilistic separation theorems, serving as a powerful tool for evaluating machine learning techniques and algorithms in complex dimensions. These theorems establish that, even with large data sets and complex dimensions, linear classifiers can effectively distinguish between incorrect and correct responses, providing crucial prerequisites for the correction of AI errors without disruption. Additionally, the report examines the practical implications of these results in both large-scale and high-dimensional environments of artificial intelligence.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling originating from a periodic potential. We utilize the density-matrix purification method to accurately calculate the ground and first excited states of a system consisting of $14$ sites for various fillings and spin-orbit coupling strengths. Utilizing a newly developed Monte Carlo technique, we determine the energy spectra with high precision. We observe the emergence of topological superfluidity accompanied by thermal phase transitions, which are revealed through calculations of the superfluid order parameter and by mapping the energy landscape onto a semi-circle of a lattice. The phase diagrams exhibit numerous complex regions, which can be explained by reducing the model to a effective one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model with arbitrary $J_{\mathrm{ex}}/\mathcal{J}$.

Consider two groups, G_1 and G_2, and suppose a homomorphism \phi from G_1 to G_2 maps a particular element to another element. In the context of graph theory, this leads to the concept of a group G_1 degrading to group G_2, which is investigated within this research. Graph degeneration is found to encompass a particular instance of this group relationship. The paper examines unique properties arising from graph degeneration. To visualize this, it employs a diagrammatic approach representing graphs realized by finite abelian groups. Order relationships within a set of all such graphs realized by finite abelian groups, based in a particular number of dimensions, are also studied and established.

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are explored, concentrating on AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities within massive Type IIA string theory. We first examine the solutions derived in four-dimensional $T^2$-wrapped form and propose a non-relativistic dual in the context of the SYM theory, whose scaling dimension we mathematically define. We further derive the 2D TQCD$_2$ dual across the massless/massive spectrum of a 2D theory resembling QCD. A prelude to prospective three-dimensional fiber-based solutions derived from string theory is provided, involving either Type II or M-theory, and an accompanying discussion on their potential in deriving a conformal 1D theory dual.

In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely depending on a well-suited kernel function. Traditionally, Gaussian Process researchers have either designed kernels from scratch, picked them from a predetermined list, or systematically searched for kernel compositions within pre-defined parameter spaces. This paper innovatively leverages Genetic-Programming, utilizing trees of fundamental mathematical expressions to represent kernel functions, thereby broadening the potential solutions, though also introducing new complexities. Our proposed method can successfully address these challenges and uncover kernel models accurately reflecting data properties. Empirically validated on real and simulated problems, this method surpasses expectations in kernel model identification, achieving notable performance enhancements in Gaussian Process-based regression and classification on diverse datasets.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to in-flight decays of
muons from the beam line, resulting in beam-induced backgrounds (BIB). This
background interference will hinder accurate data analysis and detector
operation unless mitigated. Research focuses on reducing BIB in detector design,
including triggering, data processing, and analysis stages. Studies were carried
out on a detector utilizing a tungsten nose-cone to filter BIB, utilizing
GEANT4 simulations of the CLICc concept. Analysis involved examining BIB in
critical tasks, such as lepton collisions, background levels in different
detector regions, and event selection criteria. Two scintillating technology
detectors were investigated, each optimized for distinct purposes – one for
triggering capabilities and the other for efficient data taking and background
suppression. In addition to these prototype studies, a full large-area detector
analysis was conducted, utilizing a circular geometry with enhanced BIB
suppression features. This included an advanced nose-cone design with an
optimized geometry to filter BIB, and a circular geometry extending beyond
the beam pipe to filter BIB out of the detector region. The background was then
evaluated across various run phases and demonstrated how the optimized detector
design significantly mitigates BIB, resulting in reduced backgrounds in
particle identification, trigger efficiencies, and background rejection rates in
the respective phases.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing parameters with respect to a predetermined sparsity pattern. Spartan offers flexibility in incorporating diverse sparsity policies, encompassing both random and structured sparsity, as well as cost-sensitive allocation guided by per-parameter models.
