Spartan demonstrates exceptional performance on ImageNet-1K classification, achieving significant sparsity in ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 models while maintaining accuracy within 1% of their fully dense counterparts.

The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various quantum phenomena that emerge from these interactions. A compelling example of this relationship is the behavior of a Bose gas confined to a one-dimensional space, where the presence of an infinite number of conservation laws prevents the system from reaching thermal equilibrium and constraining the system's dynamics. Through an experimental approach, our findings indicate that one-dimensional characteristics can persist into a broader three-dimensional regime, particularly in highly elongated potentials. By conducting a quench on a weakly interacting Bose gas and using Generalized Hydrodynamics to analyze its behavior, we determined that one-dimensional dephasing is the primary relaxation mechanism in this system, even when it's subjected to intense three-dimensional interactions. Notably, our research attributes this effect to the unique phenomenon of emergent Pauli blocking, where the system's internal degrees of freedom lead to a lack of accessibility to certain excited states, resulting in a specific type of scattering blockage.

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, test code that exhibits suboptimal qualities known as test smells can compromise the effectiveness of unit tests and potentially harm a project's quality if left unaddressed. Prior studies have identified multiple types of test smells, defined their characteristics, and investigated their prevalence in software systems. Despite this research, there is little scientific evidence regarding how developers subjectively assess and prioritize each test smell. This study aims to fill the gap by asking developers to rate the severity of various test smells based on their own experience with the issue, effectively shedding new light on the severity of these smells from a developmental perspective. Our results reveal that developers subjectively view Complexity Complexity as the most severe while also perceiving Branching Complexity as the least severe. Interesting patterns emerge from the correlations between developers' subjective rankings and objective data, suggesting a possible correlation between coupling and developers' subjective rankings. However, no correlation is found with object-oriented metrics nor with the size of test smell classes. From the empirical results it is also visible that developers subjectively rank biases low in Complexity Complexity while high in Branching Complexity.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s, using an integral rather than a differential measure for a moving set that varies with time. Our study also establishes the continuity of the solution with respect to initial conditions in a metric space. These findings have been further extended to address the challenge of minimizing a function by considering the behavior of its integral over all possible positions of a moving set within a specified time frame.

We introduce the updated version of {\tt KKMCee}, a Monte Carlo event generator for electron-positron pair production, which incorporates new features such as polarized quark pair production, full Standard Model cross sections, polarized cross components, inclusive and exclusive quark pair production in pairs, $Z$ boson pair production with polarization effects, $W$ boson pair production with polarized initial leptons, and their respective event generators. The polarized cross components for $h$ boson pair production are also calculated. The inclusion of these event generators in the {\tt KKMCee} toolkit expands the capabilities of Monte Carlo tools for simulating various lepton collider experiments.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, a common issue in wearable technology. We developed a highly efficient signal processing technique using the Tiramisu model to filter out background interference from ECG signals, thereby enabling accurate IBI estimation. By applying our approach to real-world datasets and comparing the results with established methods, we found that it outperformed the competitors with a significant improvement in accuracy. The success of this technique stems from the powerful capabilities of the Tiramisu model, which allows us to accurately reconstruct clean ECG signals and recover hidden features, even under adverse conditions.

To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing the communication cost associated with data transfer, especially when calculating the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in just a few data passes. The prevailing subspace randomized methods used to compute the t-SVD require 2q + 2 passes over the tensor data, where q represents a positive integer variable for iteration improvement. In this paper, we introduce a new randomized algorithm for t-SVD calculation, allowing for an arbitrary number of passes 'q', not constrained to even integers, building upon existing matrix-based approaches adapted to tensors. The error margin of the proposed method has been statistically quantified. Through practical experiments, we demonstrate that the algorithm's efficiency and usability are well-supported, and we apply this method to develop a faster computational solution for tensor completion.

Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization, but this approach struggles to accommodate dynamic behavior exhibited by real-world networks. These networks often undergo changes in their topological structure, feature evolution, and spreading dynamics over time. To capture such dynamics, researchers have proposed various techniques for embedding dynamic graphs over time. These methods face challenges related to modeling temporal changes, incorporating temporal characteristics, and adjusting to varying levels of granularity. This overview survey provides a comprehensive analysis of dynamic graph embedding by detailing its fundamental aspects and latest developments. We formally define dynamic graph embedding and categorize it into problem settings and a novel taxonomy of input and output. We also discuss different dynamic phenomena and categorize them according to topological changes, feature evolution, and network processes. In addition, we discuss various algorithmic aspects and outcomes. This work aims to provide in-depth insights into dynamic graph embedding, outlining future research directions and potential applications.

Our investigation into a $^7$H resonant state treated as a five-body system with a $^3$H core and four neutrons involved, involved constructing an effective neutron-$^3$H interaction that captures the dynamics between these particles. Through a five-body Faddeev equation treatment with a position cutoff beyond the $^3$H charge radius, we determined the energy of this resonant state to be approximately 18.7 MeV above the $^3$H ground state, consisting of a dominant $^4$N 1$^-$ and $^4$N 2$^+$ noncompact components, both of which decrease the total energy when optimized. Additionally, a narrow width of about 63 eV was derived for this resonant state within the unified theoretical framework employed.

This research paper investigates a Nirenberg type problem on the upper half spheres with the aim of finding conformal metrics that satisfy a prescribed scalar curvature and zero mean curvature on the boundary. The investigation is focused on solving a boundary equation that arises from the reduction of the main problem by differentiating the scalar curvature and the mean curvature forms. The solution of this equation allows for the decomposition of the original problem into a fixed boundary problem for the Laplacian on the half space with a homogeneous Neumann boundary condition, once an appropriate boundary metric has been established. The equation is solved using an eigenfunction expansion approach in terms of spherical harmonics. The key to the solution lies in demonstrating that under certain conditions on scalar curvature and zero mean curvature tangency, a non-trivial solution to the equation occurs. This result represents a significant development in the field of conformal geometry. The solution of the equation is local in nature and as such, is applicable in a variety of situations. One concrete consequence of our findings is that if (M^2, g) is a conformally flat hypersurface in R^3, sharing a boundary with a 1 dimensional manifold M^1 and having a constant mean curvature, then its boundary will also satisfy a constant scalar curvature, provided the above mentioned conditions are met.

Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These methods apply neural networks to embed data, with the objective of minimizing a chosen metric's differences between identical class samples and non-similar data samples. Although the Kullback-Leibler Divergence, originally suited for Poisson distributions, is frequently used, this has been proven to sometimes yield suboptimal results that contradict actual data similarities. In response, this research suggests the use of the Sinkhorn Divergence, a more reliable metric that can capture the differences in data distributions, particularly for complex Gaussian mixtures, and demonstrates its effectiveness in improving performance in several metrics. Additionally, the DOME framework is introduced, aiming to determine the optimal embeddings in a target space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These embeddings are then utilized in a variety of supervised and semi-supervised learning tasks, with the findings showing that the proposed method surpasses other deep metric learning approaches, as evident from the results on various datasets, including MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR, and SVHN.

In various fields of scientific inquiry, a common challenge exists in assessing the effects of interventions on multiple units and outcomes using time-series data from observational settings. To improve traceability and reduce the spread of infectious diseases, a series of measures were implemented in England by rapidly deploying a contact tracing system early in the pandemic. Through a hierarchical approach combining Arima-Gaussian Process modeling with a negative binomial counter, we simultaneously analyzed daily case counts and investigated the links between these outcomes and distinct local tracing measures. By employing Bayesian estimation to facilitate inference in a complex hierarchy, we effectively avoided model comparisons via post-hoc testing. Our analysis covered ninety English local authorities and three time periods. We discovered a strong link between case counts and the full local tracing service for all analyzed intervals but observed that using masks decreased new cases only in London; yet, increased adherence to isolation directives reduced new cases across all areas. Furthermore, we found that using masks and enforcing isolation both contributed to a reduced viral transmission rate but only in non-metropolitan local authorities. Our model suggested that local tracing services reduced transmission by 15.7% and that using masks and enforcing isolation each reduced transmission by 26.6% and 24.7%, respectively. Our findings have significant implications for future pandemic management, emphasizing the importance of rapidly implementing contact tracing and enforcing isolation and mask policies to curb infectious outbreaks.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides an opportunity for precise assessments of star positions, parallax, and motion based on uniform photometric data, thus enabling the determination of accurate cluster membership probabilities. Focused on the Melotte 72 open star cluster, located 2345+/-108 parsecs away and 1.0+/-0.5 billion years old, our study leverages Gaia DR2 to derive valuable cluster metrics such as radial profile, reddening, luminosity, and mass functions. Additionally, total mass and galactic coordinates are calculated. Key observations reveal that Melotte 72 displays a characteristic pattern of dynamical relaxation.

Data analysis applications in medicine, cosmology, and materials science are witnessing growing interest in probabilistic excursion patterns. This research provides the first thorough examination of Betti numbers under the condition of sparse data. Specifically, it investigates extreme values of Betti numbers as they scale with n, where a random field over a d-dimensional unit cube is defined, with our results accurate for large d in relation to n. For a standard Gaussian random field, our calculations reveal that an empirical observation-based estimate of Betti numbers accurately represents real-world findings when a certain criterion for sparsity is met, involving a trade-off between n and 1/d.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved examining the methods' performance under various noise levels and our results suggest that, in certain cases, using image information alone can provide a sufficient indicator of camera positioning.

In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to various constraints that are challenging to formalize mathematically. For instance, an RL system designed to teach a person how to cook shouldn't encourage the person to use the stove's surface for food preparation, a task that requires an understanding of physical principles and law enforcement. This paper investigates the computational feasibility of inferring constraints from observational data in reinforcement learning scenarios where actions, states, and a time limit are defined clearly. It assumes that a system's desired behavior can be represented by a set of finite Markov decision processes each with a limited number of constraints. The research initially addresses the problem of constrained RLS (Optimal Control), which aims to find the best action policy under a given set of constraints, and develops an algorithm for this purpose. While the algorithm's computational complexity grows exponentially with the number of constraints, the study demonstrates that this limitation can be mitigated by learning a compact representation of the system's dynamics through a simplified neural network structure. The paper also addresses the problem of inferring all constraints in a given set of MDPs and provides a computational lower bound on the computational efficiency of this task.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will chart our galaxy's structure using intense, all-sky observations of the 1 billion stars in the nearby universe, mapping their positions, motions, and brightnesses with high precision. Launched in 2013 as part of the COSMOS family of space missions, the mission will create a detailed three-dimensional chart of the galaxy's structure near us and provide a unique understanding of its composition and the universe's dark matter. This report summarizes the mission's objectives and demonstrates how its findings will significantly contribute to multiple fields of astrophysics.

For graphs with a given number of vertices and treewidth of order $O(n^{1/2-\epsilon})$, we have devised a word-RAM algorithm to compute vertex separators in $O(n)$ bits. Furthermore, we can apply our algorithm to compute an $O(1)$-approximation for tree decomposition in time $c^k n (\log \log n) / \log^{1+\epsilon} n$, still requiring $O(n)$ bits. In both cases, provided $k > 0$ and $\epsilon > 0$, we could achieve any constant $c > 1$. The proof of the first result relies on combining Chlamtac and Svitkovas' separator and the planar partition approach developed by Abbott et al. The second result arises from combining the first with an efficient algorithm for planar partition due to Abbott et al.

A substantial portion of network information comes from edge weights and their directionality.
Most network measures were initially developed for simple undirected networks.
As a result, weighted network extensions were created to incorporate weight-based information, particularly for calculating the local clustering coefficient.
We discovered that not all these extensions consider the weights fully; some depend on the degree and react sensitively to even small weight changes, a limitation we call "hybrid."
For many scenarios, we advocate using fully-weighted definitions.
We specify requirements for effectively analyzing multiple weighted networks, and propose a new continuous clustering coefficient that meets all the criteria and handles vanishing weights.
We show through synthetic and real-world examples that our continuous clustering coefficient offers better results and its behavior provides valuable insights in situations like noisy networks, heterogeneous systems, and networks derived from inference.

One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about system or material behavior into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been used across a variety of applications including solid mechanics, fluid mechanics, and fluid-structure interactions. While PINNs have primarily been used as a training technique to incorporate known data and boundary conditions, they also enable the derivation of error estimates using the training data, which can offer several advantages. This study calculates a posteriori error estimates valid for any physics-informed neural network, including PINNs, without imposing specific smoothness requirements on the remaining boundary conditions. The proposed error estimates are evaluated in terms of simplicity, adaptability, and practical applicability through numerical examples involving a variety of partial and ordinary differential equations.

For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. With the advancement of computational power and accessible large datasets, machine learning and big data analysis have significantly improved our capabilities in this area. This discussion outlines the recent developments and future opportunities for incorporating geostatistics and machine learning approaches in air pollution modeling. We provide a comprehensive review of current methodologies and offer suggestions for future strategies focused on spatial data integration and model evaluation.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohmic dissipation). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in this scenario by localized tunneling, other non-Majorana features involve delocalized tunneling. By comparing conductance at normal and high-resistance leads under identical non-Majorana conditions, one can determine if the zero-energy peak persists in the high-resistance setup. If it does, this suggests the presence of a topological superconductor containing Majorana zero modes.

We have established a non-asymptotic lower bound for the eight actions case in the linear bandit problem, and shown it to be tight in terms of its coefficients. Specifically, we have demonstrated that any algorithm employing $T$ trials to determine the optimal action across multiple $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_8$ means, while selecting $n_t$ instances for each $\mu_i$, will face a probability lower than some constant of correctly identifying the optimal action in the last $T_0(T_0=O(T^{1/4}))$ trials, given a sufficiently large total number $n$ of instances. This lower bound matches the performance of an efficient fully informative, i.i.d. inference algorithm we introduced, which correctly identifies the optimal action in $T_0$ trials, given a sufficiently large $T$. This result holds for any non-asymptotic analysis, including those in relative settings, and we have similar conclusions for $d>8$ actions case. We have derived analogous lower bounds for $d>8$ actions case. These findings imply that our previously proposed, highly informative algorithms, initially proven to be near-optimal in low-dimensional settings, are not only near-optimal but also the first to solve certain bandit problems with rich action sets over linear models. These conclusions also apply to corank matrices with a limited rank. Additionally, we have made a novel connection between certain bandit problems with rich action sets and inference problems,

Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, exhibiting distinct behavior in separate electron bands.  Yet, the same gaps that drive the valley effect also make the orbital momentum a more relevant and sensitive parameter. This work demonstrates that an external field's influence on orbital momentum produces an orbital Hall effect in graphene that differs from the valley Hall effect in terms of its charge carrier distribution. Notably, the orbital Hall effect can be identified through its resistance to magnetic rotation, thereby offering potential applications in spin-based electronics due to its increased stability.

The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. This work aims to explore the novel threat of data manipulation during training (Data Poisoning) targeting Graph Classification neural networks via Reinforcement Learning agents.

The process of matching object groups in two catalogues can be improved by enhancing the identification of true astrometric and photometric counterparts using statistical probability models. The existing standards for a match being "probable" or "definite" may lead to a loss of information, as the probability distribution of potential matches is partially utilized. By utilizing the entire probability distribution, the risks associated with false positives or false negatives can be quantified. A normalizing flow is presented as a technique to determine a matching probability for each object pair, accounting for observational noise in both astrometry and photometry. This new framework is applied to a sample of likely dual optical/Infrared identifications from the ATLAS legacy project and showcases its effectiveness in a real-world demonstration, also including discussions of key assumptions and characterizations of the statistical models.

In this paper, a hypergraph is considered as the family of its edges, and a hypergraph is said to possess property C(k, ρ) if the size of the intersection of all its sub-graphs of size k is less than ρ. A vertex cover of a hypergraph is a subset of vertices that intersects with every edge, and a hypergraph is said to have the C(k, ρ) property if the size of the intersection of all its sub-graphs of size k is less than ρ. A vertex cover of size n is called k-extendable if it can be expanded to a vertex cover of size n + k using at most ρ new vertices. The authors demonstrate that for infinitely large hypergraphs, a vertex cover is either complete or nearly k-extendable and possessing property C(k, ρ) with ρ being a function of n and the remainder when n is divided by k.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. A user study and system demonstration will be conducted to evaluate the introduction of this novel visualisation method.

We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to enhance semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss promotes consistent pronunciation within a training dataset without explicit annotation, utilizing a pre-trained language model, while CycleGAN leverages data augmentation and a cycle-consistency constraint to refine the speech-to-text mapping. Our proposed method integrates these techniques with a conventional end2end trainer, demonstrating significant improvement over inter-domain loss alone and exhibiting comparable performance to the baseline. Furthermore, Inter-domain loss and CycleGAN exhibit complementary benefits when used in conjunction, illustrating the potential for gainful interactions between different approaches.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system.

Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions.

The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper sets out to dispute the prevailing notion that larger models necessarily lead to better performance in Automated Essay Scoring. To this end, the study puts multiple base models with differing numbers of parameters through various tests, employing not only exact mimics of prominent NLP models but also more efficient variants to reduce computational costs. The paper's central argument is that better performance can be achieved by using smaller, more efficient models.

One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in target domains using unsupervised methods.  To address this challenge, we transform the object detection task into a ranking task among positive and negative boxes, turning false positive suppression into an efficient box re-ranking problem without the need for manual annotation.  A secondary challenge in this process is the absence of labeled samples in the source domain as well.  To address this, we introduce a self-training strategy within the framework of the pseudo label method to create supervisory signals from labeled boxes in the source domain, training a feature extractor that adapts to target domains.  A subsequent ranking module, trained with the self-developed supervisory signals, performs effectively in box re-ranking.  Our self-supervised approach achieves first place in the TED 2022 benchmark for unsupervised domain adaptive pedestrian detection.

This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo effects, and microphone distortion. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation called the mel-spectrogram into a new, more desirable format, and another converts synthetically created mel-spectrograms into high-quality audio waves that are perceptually natural-sounding. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses established methods, which apply more conventional techniques for reversing the mel-spectrogram process and another technique directly translating noisy audio waves to clear ones. Moreover, the research also examines the dependability of typical audio improvement evaluation metrics in the context of music by conducting a listening test.

The primary objective of this study is to expand the application of motion editing techniques to throwing movements, allowing for the creation of realistic and aesthetically pleasing effects. Although point of release is a key element in defining a throwing motion, current capture and editing systems either fix its position or require significant artist input to determine it. Our novel system, called FauxThrow, automates the calculation of the point of release for a given throwing motion. By optimizing a virtual object's rotation and position over time, FauxThrow identifies a plausible point of release that adheres to physical laws and creates a realistic throwing motion appearance, even when the object's dynamics are not accurately simulated. Additionally, FauxThrow permits artists to incorporate user-specified points of release during the throwing motion, enabling the attainment of intricate and custom effects. Our qualitative evaluation reveals that the point of release has a significant impact on the overall appearance of the throwing motion, and FauxThrow successfully produces novel and engaging effects, as demonstrated by our quantitative comparisons of released and non-released trajectories.

To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN has been designed, which leverages a tree-structured DRNN (Doubly-Recurrent Neural Networks) model originally proposed in 2016 by Alvarez-Melis and Jaakola. The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture synergizes a sequential encoder with tree-structured decoding enhanced by a syntax-aware attention mechanism, differing from prior syntax-based NMT methods that rely on dependency parsing models. Conversely, the presented approach utilizes constituency parsing models, which it posits provides valuable information for translation. Moreover, by incorporating syntactic sentence structure, additional connections are established within the Seq2DRNN+SynC decoder neural network. Comparative evaluations demonstrate that the proposed Seq2DRNN architecture yields more natural translations and exhibits superior reordering abilities in comparison to sequential and state-of-the-art syntax-based NMT models. Consequently, it outperforms other models in both translation and constituency parsing tasks.

The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse structures and energy patterns found at ice-grain surface binding sites. Currently, there are no publicly accessible databases of binding energies that capture this complexity. Our study creates such a database by gathering and standardizing experimental and theoretical binding energy values for 130 different molecule-species pairings on various ice surfaces. To ensure high precision in our results, all theoretical values were calculated using multiple quantum chemical methods and basis sets, yielding multiple calculations for each binding site and molecule combination. Our findings show that the ice surface characteristics, such as hydrogen bonding patterns and chemical compositions, has a significant impact on the binding energies. The database, referred to as the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform, is available online and includes the relevant theoretical and experimental data, allowing for its direct use in astrochemical models. This resource will be particularly useful for future studies focusing on interstellar complex organic molecules and their applications in theoretical astrochemistry.

A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a theoretical model of the process is developed and its distribution, characterized by four parameters, along with its statistical properties, is analytically determined. This model is further validated by demonstrating its compatibility with real-world data through parameter adjustment.

We offer novel approaches to acquire in-depth knowledge about a mysterious quantum state using an efficiently manageable number of copies. Our key contribution is a depth-controlled randomized measurement technique that generates expectations based on state expectations. Our research demonstrates that this approach can be successfully applied to determine key properties of arbitrary states, achieve improved bounds for the quantum Chernoff inequality, and precisely calculate the trace of a mysterious quantum operator with target errors in polynomial time. These advances are fueled by our diverse set of randomly constructed quantum circuits generated using the random Clifford circuit model, which we found has numerous applications across our research.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specified reference \cite{KlSjSt20}. They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries.

The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need to preserve the original class label. In order to overcome this constraint, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the use of data transforms that can vary class labels and enable the expansion of coverage of input data. To this end, we provide a comprehensive framework that encompasses a broad range of data transforms that encompass popular existing techniques as special cases. Specifically, we introduce a novel family of unsupervised transforms that can be learned from unlabeled data and vary class labels, which includes the unsupervised version of our previous work. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these transforms in our experiments on six datasets, showing that they outperform the original supervised transforms while achieving better results than many other classification baselines.

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study offers: 1) a new algorithm called MUSE, 2) a thorough understanding of its performance, and 3) proven guarantees for its effectiveness. Moreover, we show that MUSE can learn the underlying low-dimensional representation consistently across numerous tasks. Our investigation also exposes the limitations of previous methods in the real world and provides justifications for their shortcomings.

Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it's discovered that distillation-based model performance variability heavily relies on several preconditions, making it a somewhat unreliable compression approach. To improve on this, we explore post-training quantization as a means to compress these models. Ultimately, while distillation was found effective in certain low-resource languages, it's shown that quantization produces more consistent performance outcomes across a broader range of languages, particularly those with the least available training data.

The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain cases and show that the Lagrangian density of a specific 3-uniform graph is sqrt(3)/3, resulting in an irrational Turan density, which answers an open question posed by Baber and Talbot.

The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. By training fully convolutional neural network models on subsets of various sizes from a total dataset, each model undergoes a different image enhancement while its performance is compared to a baseline model trained without such augmentations on the entire dataset. Ultimately, we discovered that using zooming and rotating image enhancements yields a significant reduction of 80% in labelled data requirements while maintaining at least 0.96 AUC and 0.41 F1-Score in comparison to a baseline model trained with 100 labelled images.

Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to the desired style and level of detail. This paper proposes a unified image captioning framework that excels across various domains and can effortlessly adapt to multiple captioning styles. We incorporate a flexible prompt learning system that enables the model to absorb data from multiple domains, ensuring its performance remains strong in each domain. Additionally, we optimize the prompts using dynamic vectors within a word embedding space, reducing the reliance on manual tuning and significantly enhancing the model's capabilities. At the inference stage, our model allows for the generation of custom caption styles by simply selecting the most suitable prompt, yielding outstanding results in COCO Karpathy and TextCaps benchmarks.

As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. By applying the formal definition of harm based on causal models and actual causality, it becomes possible to distinguish between different forms of harm. The distinction between intervention-based and non-intervention-based harm reveals that self-inflicted harm is uniquely characterized by its intentional nature. Furthermore, this new understanding of harm enables the differentiation between its subtle forms, allowing for a more comprehensive range of applications, including but not limited to, scenarios involving privacy breaches.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Cognitive Toolkit and Apache Spark by introducing Java bindings and new components. The integration with OpenCV and the development of automated PySpark wrapper generation tool expands the capabilities of Spark's ecosystem. The MMLSpark library is accompanied by an extensive collection of tools and features. To demonstrate the potential of this collaboration, we develop a full-scale solution for automatically classifying Snow Leopards using camera trap images and apply it in a real-world setting.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly valuable for language pairs with limited speech-to-text data, yet we still observe a performance gap compared to models fine-tuned for speech-to-text on existing datasets.

This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly during peak hours when load demands are at their highest. In conjunction with normal load forecasts, predictive models aiming to anticipate these peak hours are crucial in helping network operators optimize distribution, especially when it comes to identifying whether peaks are likely to occur and at what time they might arise. Although there's a lack of standardized methods for making peak hour forecasts, they're becoming increasingly important due to rising levels of distributed power sources and flexible load components. In this research, we combine probabilistic load forecasts from ensemble learning with a machine learning-based routine for extracting peak hours from smart meter data. Our method is tested using data from 15,517 smart meters across three countries and validated through analysis of actual consumption data and discussion with practitioners and researchers in the field. Our results indicate that integrating peak hour forecasts into probabilistic load forecasting can lead to more accurate and reliable forecasts, especially concerning peak hour predictions.

The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and insufficient resources. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can address some of these challenges to a degree. The difficulty in effectively integrating knowledge lies in the multiple forms of knowledge representation involved. This paper aims to provide an overview of various knowledge integration approaches and their effectiveness in machine learning applications.

Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite considerable advancements. The issue often arises due to annotation biases affecting traditional supervised segmentation techniques, which rely on detailed boundary markings. To resolve these issues and minimize labeling expenses, we introduce an innovative framework that utilizes image-level labels, thereby facilitating unbiased lesion detection and reducing data annotation costs. This data-driven framework pairs a generative adversarial network with a specialized decoder to distinguish lesions from the original images. Our experiments using two COVID-19 datasets confirm the efficiency and superior performance of this new approach compared to existing methods.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. Existing automated methods either perform well in average spine positions but struggle with deviation-induced errors, or rely on reliable initializations which are often unreliable in challenging cases. To address these limitations, we introduce an effective and flexible optimization-based strategy to correctly position and order $L$ vertebrae in CT scans. By combining rectification strategy with anatomically-constrained optimization, we achieve notable improvements (4.2% and 3.9% reduction in error rate, respectively, compared to state-of-the-art techniques), while ensuring widespread applicability and ease of training. Additionally, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in combining optimization strategy with image features.

Our theory explores the behavior of electron collisions with a strong electric field in a confined space near extremely strong interactions between light and matter. The resulting reaction can take on two forms: either a steady state forms and traps the electron, or a stable equilibrium state forms and stabilizes the system. The steady state has the potential to trap the electron due to a local minimum in the energy landscape and this has been mathematically modeled using a Wigner function. On the other hand, the stable equilibrium state has the potential to trap the electron due to a shift in the location of its energy levels and this has been modeled using a specific form of light-matter coupling. The electron's energy also changes due to a shift in its phase and this has the potential to make the system stable. The behavior of light due to this strong interaction is described using a specific mathematical framework in terms of modes and their associated coefficients. The behavior of light in this strong interaction is described using a specific mathematical framework in terms of modes and their associated coefficients.

In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We've adopted an learning-based approach to control a all-terrain quadruped equipped with series-series actuators, which can take advantage of its elastic properties. Our method integrates a reinforcement learning-based controller with a model-predictive framework with a pre-trained policy, pre-trained online policy updates, and an intrinsic exploration strategy to increase efficiency. Our experiments on various outdoor terrains shew that leveraging the actuator's elasticity leads to enhanced movement performance and a balance between efficiency and energy consumption.

We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with minimal deviation in Hilbert-Schmidt distance. Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via simulations that utilize state vectors and random quantum measurements. These simulations demonstrate that VSV efficiently detects separability, yields accurate results even with limited resources, and exhibits scalable performance in terms of qubit count. Next, we develop a set of metrics to measure state provability and determinism, showing that most feasible instances of NQUBIT GHZ states can be solved with significantly less noise tolerance than the quasiclassical threshold. Our algorithm's conceptual framework for dealing with noisy quantum states serves as a model for handling highly complicated states, while its performance serves as a benchmark for further advancements in quantum algorithms.

A well-documented phenomenon, microtearing modes, occurs due to the electron temperature gradient in a plasma and causes fine-scale magnetic reconnections and the formation of magnetic islands. Prior research in a slab geometry setting showed that the drive mechanism requires collisions, but our simulations show that in the absence of collisions, there is still a small-scale, electron-driven tearing instability that exists. Detailed studies reveal that these modes have physical properties similar to larger, collision-driven modes, including how they behave dynamically, what drives their instability, and their effect on magnetic field topology. Interestingly, these modes have little impact on the overall magnetic energy distribution but influence the formation of small-scale structures.

A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the difficulty in defining attributes and preserving query uniqueness. Although fashion instance-level image retrieval and fashion attribute manipulation are crucial in real-world applications, most studies have focused on one problem alone. In this research, we aim to achieve state-of-the-art results on both tasks. To accomplish this, we propose a novel method that translates a query into a representation that incorporates the desired attributes. By introducing feature-level attribute manipulation, we match the manipulated features with real ones, allowing for independent attribute manipulation from the underlying representation. This breakthrough empowers existing image retrieval methods to perform attribute manipulation without compromising retrieval performance.

The $\R$-optimal solution for the classical underdetermined system $Ax=y$ with an approximate vector $\hat{y}$ is the minimizer of the functional $\frac{\|x\|_X^p}{p}$ subject to the constraint $\|Ax-y\|_{Y^*}^q\leq q$. By substituting the Euler-Lagrange equation, we obtain a fixed-point problem involving an implicitly defined function $\Rbar$ and its Jacobian $\Jbar$, where the norm of $\Rbar'$ is bounded, making the sequence of iterates produced by the dual gradient scheme $(1+\alpha)\Rbar_z(\Rbar'(z)-\hat{y})-z$ converge to the $\R$-optimal solution for a sufficiently small step-size $\alpha$. Moreover, we prove that the dual scheme has asymptotic linear convergence, where the constant is independent of the parameters and the norms involved, provided certain conditions on $\hat{y}$ and the source angle are met. We present numerical results for a linear inverse problem in Partial Differential Equations, where the data involves a space with a singular source and the solution lies in a space with a p-integral mean on a ball. Furthermore, we demonstrate the recovery of the inclusion boundary from partial data using the dual scheme.

Constructing the matching cost matrix is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost matrices by sampling matching pixels in each sub-aperture, but this approach is flawed as it treats all pixels equally regardless of their level of occlusion, which can result in distorted cost matrices and impaired estimated depths. In response to this issue, we propose a novel, deep learning-based method for constructing the matching cost matrix, which incorporates an autonomous module for identifying occluded pixels to weight samples appropriately. Our approach has been validated through experiments on existing and newly collected datasets, which demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms by maintaining high efficiency as well. The source code for our approach can be found at the repository located at https://github.com/ChengWeixuan/LFD_OA_CC.

This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis and contour integration. Furthermore, the paper examines periodic solution properties over an extended period.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results.

To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve their performance, including their ability to maintain connectivity and data transfer. As these networks become increasingly congested, delivering certain data services on time can become a significant issue. To mitigate this problem, this study proposes an intelligent access point (AP) and extender selection mechanism that ensures reliable and timely data transfer in these networks. The proposed system is based on the IEEE 802.11k/v standards, which allow WiFi networks to optimize their configuration and performance. The proposed solution involves two main components: the first calculates the delay between a device and the nearest AP or extender, and the second determines the optimal AP or extender for each data packet transmission, taking into account the packet's size and the number of remaining hops. The proposed system is implemented and evaluated using a network simulator, and its effectiveness and performance are confirmed through simulations and comparisons with other existing methods.
